title: Page Seven
passage:
Since March, your Saturday paper has given page seven to "Good News". I read it every week. Last Saturday it had a dog that pulled a swimmer from a lake and a grandmother who ran a marathon at ninety. They were lovely stories. I had forgotten both by Sunday lunch.

Good news and bad news often move at different speeds. A fire or a crash happens in one afternoon, so it fits on page one. Much of the best news happens slowly. Worldwide, the share of children who die before their fifth birthday has more than halved since 1990. That is enormous, but it happened a little every year, and no single day of it was ever a story.

I know you cannot print "Things slightly better again" every morning. Nobody would buy that paper. But a brave dog is just the cheerful version of a fire: something sudden. Page seven makes me smile. It has not once made me think the world is better than page one says.
question: What is the writer's main point?
correct: The page can't balance the bad news, because it reports sudden events and the biggest improvements are slow.
wrong1: The page can't balance the bad news, because readers forget happy stories faster than sad ones.
wrong2: The page can't balance the bad news, because papers print far more sad stories than happy ones.
wrong3: The page helps to balance the bad news, because small happy stories remind readers that good things happen.
explanation: In paragraph 2, the best news happens "a little every year", so no day of it is "ever a story". In paragraph 3, the brave dog is "something sudden", just like a fire, so the page cannot change what page one says.
source: Original letter; the newspaper and its stories are imagined. Real fact: the global under-five mortality rate fell by more than half between 1990 and the early 2020s (about 93 to under 40 deaths per 1,000 live births; UNICEF / UN Inter-agency Group for Child Mortality Estimation).
question2: Why did the writer write this letter?
correct2: To criticise a new page in the paper, even though its stories are enjoyable.
wrong1_2: To thank the paper for a new page, even though the writer soon forgets its stories.
wrong2_2: To ask the paper to report more slow improvements, like the fall in child deaths.
wrong3_2: To explain why fires and crashes are easier to report than other news.
explanation2: The writer calls the stories "lovely" but says the page has "not once" changed how the world looks next to page one.

title: Forty Cats
passage:
For two years I posted a drawing online every day, usually of buildings: bus stops, old shop fronts, the water tower near my flat. Each one got about thirty likes, mostly from the same friends. Then one evening I drew my cat asleep in a cereal box. By morning it had four thousand.

When I look back at the next two months, I count forty cats. I never decided to stop drawing buildings. Each morning I sat down with my pencil, and the cat just seemed like the obvious thing to draw. The buildings started to feel like homework.

People often warn that likes make us anxious or unhappy. I kept waiting for that feeling, and it never came. I slept well and felt fine all summer, which is probably why I didn't notice anything. Last week I hid the numbers. This morning I drew the bus stop on Carter Street again, and I have no idea how many people liked it.
question: What does the writer want readers to understand?
correct: The thousands of likes quietly changed what the writer drew, and feeling fine hid the change.
wrong1: The thousands of likes did the writer no real harm, because the writer felt fine all summer.
wrong2: The thousands of likes made the writer anxious, so the writer drew cats to get more.
wrong3: The thousands of likes showed the writer that people liked cats much more than buildings.
explanation: In paragraph 2 the writer counts "forty cats" but "never decided" to stop drawing buildings. In paragraph 3 the writer "felt fine all summer", which is why the writer "didn't notice anything".
source: Original. Imagined artist and blog post.
question2: How is the passage organised?
correct2: A sudden success, the next two months, then a familiar warning and a small change.
wrong1_2: A familiar warning about likes, the writer's own story, then advice for other artists.
wrong2_2: A problem with likes, several things the writer tried, then the one that worked.
wrong3_2: Two kinds of drawing compared, then the writer's reasons for choosing one of them.
explanation2: The cat drawing comes first, then "the next two months", then a warning about likes and the writer's decision to hide the numbers.

title: The Second Time
passage:
My brother refuses to read anything about a film before he sees it. No trailers, no reviews, not even the poster. Last year a colleague told him how a detective film ended, and he was angry with her for a week.

I understand the feeling. I once learned the ending of a famous ghost story too early, and I'll never know what that first surprise would have felt like. But people watch their favourite films again and again, knowing every line. Small children ask for the same bedtime story every night and complain if you change a word. If knowing the ending destroyed a story, none of this would happen.

My brother watched the detective film a month later. He said it was boring and blamed his colleague. I've seen it too. For ninety minutes nobody does anything interesting, and the twist in the last five is the only reason to stay awake. I don't think the spoiler took much away from him. There wasn't much there to take.
question: Which sentence best sums up what the writer is saying?
correct: Films that a spoiler can ruin have little to offer apart from the surprise.
wrong1: Films lose nothing important when viewers already know how the story will end.
wrong2: Films with a twist deserve to be watched without anyone revealing the ending first.
wrong3: Films are often more enjoyable the second time, when viewers know every line.
explanation: Paragraph 2 says people watch favourite films "again and again, knowing every line". In paragraph 3 the twist is "the only reason to stay awake", so "There wasn't much there to take."
source: Original. Imagined family and film.
question2: What is the writer mainly trying to do?
correct2: To challenge a common complaint, using one spoiled film as the main example.
wrong1_2: To defend a common habit, using the writer's brother as the main example.
wrong2_2: To explain why people enjoy watching their favourite films again and again.
wrong3_2: To warn readers not to tell their friends or colleagues how a film ends.
explanation2: The writer questions the brother's anger by showing that the detective film had little to offer apart from its twist.

title: The Last Edition
passage:
The Valley Courier closed last spring after 112 years. For a few weeks, people in the town said they missed it: the football results, the photos of school concerts, the notices of births and deaths. Then an online neighbourhood group took over most of that. Parents posted their own concert photos, and clubs posted their own scores, usually faster than the paper ever had.

Nobody posted about the council. For thirty years, a Courier reporter called Mary Osei had sat through every council meeting, three hours on a Tuesday evening, writing down who voted for what. Very few people read her reports. The editor once admitted they were the least popular page in the paper.

In May, the council agreed to sell the land under the old swimming pool to a builder. It was all done at a normal public meeting, with the doors open. Most people in town found out in September, when the fences went up. Nobody had hidden anything. Nobody had been there to write it down.
question: What does the writer want readers to understand?
correct: When the paper closed, its least-read reporting turned out to be the part nobody replaced.
wrong1: When the paper closed, an online group quickly took over the pages people liked most.
wrong2: When the paper closed, the online group let the town down by ignoring the council.
wrong3: When the paper closed, the council used the silence to make its decisions in secret.
explanation: In paragraph 1 an online group "took over most of that". Paragraph 2 says the council reports were "the least popular page", and in paragraph 3 "Nobody had been there to write it down."
source: Original. Imagined newspaper, town and reporter.
question2: Why did the writer write this text?
correct2: To show, through one town's story, what a town loses when its paper closes.
wrong1_2: To show, through one town's story, how quickly people can replace a local paper.
wrong2_2: To praise a reporter who spent thirty years writing reports that few people read.
wrong3_2: To criticise a council for selling public land without telling anyone.
explanation2: The writer follows one town from the paper's closing to the day "the fences went up", to show what was lost with it.

title: Series Three
passage:
The first series of The Long Table sounded like nothing on paper: eight amateur carpenters in a barn, each building one piece of furniture a week. Nobody shouted. When a young nurse cut a table leg too short, the retired builder at the next bench put down his own tools and helped her fix it. That clip was shared everywhere.

Series three has a ticking clock in the corner of the screen, a "surprise twist" in every episode and loud drums whenever someone picks up a saw. Contestants are now interviewed alone and asked who they think should go home. Most of them look uncomfortable. They try to say something kind, and then they give a name.

The new tasks are clever, I'll admit, and the furniture has never been better. But I didn't watch the first series for the furniture. This week, a teacher's chair collapsed halfway through the final task. Everyone looked up as it fell. Then they looked back at their own clocks.
question: What is the writer's main point?
correct: The show's new drama has pushed out the kindness that made the first series worth watching.
wrong1: The show has got worse because the furniture is not as good as it used to be.
wrong2: The show is better than before overall, though it has lost some of its gentle charm.
wrong3: The show's new contestants are less kind than the people in the first series were.
explanation: In paragraph 1 a builder "helped her fix it". After the changes in paragraph 2, nobody helps the teacher in paragraph 3, and they look "back at their own clocks".
source: Original. Imagined television series.
question2: How does the writer build the review?
correct2: The first series, the changes since, then one fair point and one scene.
wrong1_2: The changes in series three, the problems they cause, then ideas for fixing them.
wrong2_2: Praise for series three, one small complaint, then a fair point about the furniture.
wrong3_2: One contestant's journey through the series, from the first week to the last.
explanation2: The review starts with series one, describes the changes in series three, then admits the tasks are "clever" before a scene from this week.

title: Three Questions
passage:
Lara's job was to look after the comments under articles on a small news site, and for years they were a battlefield. She tried everything. She deleted rude posts, but new ones arrived faster than she could read them. She made people comment under their real names, and they went on arguing under their real names.

Then she tried something much smaller. Before you could comment, you had to answer three easy questions about the article. Which city was the story about? Who was the woman in the photo? Anyone who had read it could answer in ten seconds.

The number of comments fell by more than half. The ones that were left were longer and calmer, and people disagreed with each other politely. When Lara looked at who had stopped commenting, she recognised many of the names. They were the people who had once written long, furious replies to things the articles had never said.
question: Which sentence best sums up what the writer is saying?
correct: The quiz worked because many of the angriest commenters had never read the articles.
wrong1: The quiz worked because answering it slowed people down long enough to calm down.
wrong2: The quiz worked because rude commenters found the questions too hard to answer.
wrong3: The quiz worked because fewer comments meant fewer posts for the angry people to answer.
explanation: Paragraph 2 says anyone "who had read it" could answer in seconds. In paragraph 3, the people who stopped had replied "to things the articles had never said".
source: Original. Imagined news site and moderator.
question2: How is the passage organised?
correct2: A problem, two attempts that failed, a small change, then what it showed.
wrong1_2: A problem, the reasons for it, then some rules for other news websites.
wrong2_2: A small change, the problems it caused, then how Lara solved them.
wrong3_2: Two news websites compared, then a judgement about which one is better.
explanation2: Paragraph 1 gives the problem and two failed ideas, paragraph 2 the quiz, and paragraph 3 what Lara learned from it.

title: After Six O'Clock
passage:
Children's television ended at six o'clock when I was small. A presenter waved, a clock appeared on the screen, and the news began. Nobody had to switch anything off. The programme did it for us, and we went off to find something else to do.

My daughter watches videos on a tablet, and much of what she watches is better than anything I had: real scientists, clever cartoons, a woman in Nairobi who teaches her to draw birds. When I first worried about screens, I worried about what was on them. I read reviews and blocked channels, and mostly I stopped worrying.

Her videos don't end. When one finishes, the next has already started, chosen for her. Every evening, somewhere in the middle of a video about penguins or volcanoes, I say "That's enough now", and she looks at me as if I've switched off the sun.
question: What does the writer want readers to understand?
correct: Online videos never stop by themselves, so ending them has become a parent's job.
wrong1: Online videos are better than old television, so children now want to watch for longer.
wrong2: Online videos are fine for children, as long as parents choose the channels carefully.
wrong3: Online videos choose what children watch next, so parents can no longer control what they see.
explanation: In paragraph 1, "The programme did it for us." In paragraph 3, "Her videos don't end", so now the writer has to say "That's enough now" every evening.
source: Original. Imagined family.
question2: How does the writer build the passage?
correct2: A childhood memory, praise for today's videos, then a problem the past did not have.
wrong1_2: A childhood memory, problems with today's videos, then a list of rules for parents.
wrong2_2: Praise for today's videos, a childhood memory, then advice on choosing good channels.
wrong3_2: Old and new children's programmes compared, then a judgement on which is better.
explanation2: Paragraph 1 remembers six o'clock, paragraph 2 praises what the daughter watches, and paragraph 3 shows something new the writer must do every evening.

title: The Laughing Machine
passage:
In the 1950s, an American sound engineer called Charles Douglass built a machine full of recorded laughter. Television producers used it to add laughs to comedy shows, and for decades viewers at home heard an audience that wasn't there. Today the idea seems a little embarrassing, and many modern comedies are proud to have no laugh track at all.

Meanwhile, millions of people watch reaction videos, in which someone films themselves watching a funny clip. Often the clip sits in a small box in the corner, and the laughing face fills the rest of the screen. Plenty of people who make fun of old laugh tracks watch these every day.

Researchers who study laughter have found that we laugh far more often with other people than alone. A comedy watched alone on a sofa is missing something, and Douglass's machine was built to supply it. Of course, his laughs had been recorded earlier, for other jokes. The face in the corner is at least laughing at this one.
question: What is the writer's main point?
correct: Reaction videos give people watching alone someone to laugh with, just as laugh tracks once did.
wrong1: Reaction videos are popular because, unlike laugh tracks, the laughter in them is real.
wrong2: Reaction videos are as embarrassing as laugh tracks, and people will soon mock them too.
wrong3: Reaction videos are popular because people enjoy watching faces more than the jokes themselves.
explanation: Paragraph 1 says the machine gave viewers "an audience that wasn't there". Paragraph 3 says we laugh more "with other people than alone", and the face in the corner does the same job.
source: Real facts: Charles Douglass, an American sound engineer, invented the laugh-track machine (the 'laff box') in the early 1950s (widely documented, e.g. obituaries in 2003). That people laugh far more often in company than alone is a well-established finding (Robert Provine's research on laughter). Reaction videos are a widely known online genre; no claims about any real creator or company.
question2: How is the passage organised?
correct2: An old invention, a modern habit, then a finding that links the two.
wrong1_2: An old invention, the reasons it failed, then the habit that replaced it.
wrong2_2: A modern habit, the case against it, then the writer's defence of it.
wrong3_2: Two kinds of comedy show compared, then a judgement on which is funnier.
explanation2: Paragraph 1 describes the laugh machine, paragraph 2 reaction videos, and paragraph 3 a research finding that connects them.

title: Dog Ears
passage:
My niece is fourteen, and half the photos she sends me have dog ears in them. Sometimes she is a cat or a cartoon princess with enormous eyes. When these filters first appeared, I worried. Now I think they are the healthiest pictures on her phone.

The ones that worry me are the others. Another popular kind of filter is almost invisible. It makes skin a little smoother and eyes a little bigger. Her friends use it in almost every photo, and my niece wasn't sure which of her own pictures had it on.

Nobody looks at themselves with dog ears and thinks, "Why don't I look like that?" Everyone is in on the joke. Slightly smoother skin is different: it looks like a real face on a good day. People edited photos long before phones, of course, and magazines did far worse. But a magazine cover was one face on a shop shelf. This is every face in her class, every day.
question: Which sentence best sums up what the writer is saying?
correct: Filters that look natural do more harm than silly ones, because nobody notices them working.
wrong1: Silly filters are healthy, because they help young people laugh at the way they look.
wrong2: Filters are nothing new to worry about, since magazines edited photos far more before phones.
wrong3: Filters harm teenagers' confidence, whether they add dog ears or make skin look smoother.
explanation: Paragraph 1 calls the silly pictures "the healthiest pictures on her phone". Paragraphs 2 and 3 show that the other filter is "almost invisible" and "looks like a real face".
source: Original. Imagined family. General, widely known facts only: phone apps offer both novelty filters and appearance-smoothing filters; photo retouching long predates phones.
question2: What is the writer mainly trying to do?
correct2: To explain why the writer has changed their mind about photo filters.
wrong1_2: To complain that teenagers now put filters on almost every photo they share.
wrong2_2: To describe how phone filters change the shape and skin of people's faces.
wrong3_2: To explain why the writer has stopped worrying about teenagers' photo filters.
explanation2: The writer once worried about the silly filters, then explains why "The ones that worry me are the others".

title: The 1 a.m. Version of Me
passage:
I joined a new video app in January and followed accounts about cooking, Spanish grammar and old buildings. I wanted to learn things. For about a week, that is exactly what the app showed me.

Then exams started, and so did the late nights. At one in the morning, too tired to study and too awake to sleep, I didn't want grammar. I watched a man pressure-washing a dirty driveway, then another, then about twenty more. I never searched for them. I just didn't scroll past.

Now my feed is mostly driveways, even at lunchtime, when the clever daytime version of me opens the app hoping for Spanish. I can't really blame it. It isn't wrong about me: I watched every one of those videos to the end. I could follow more Spanish accounts, I suppose. I followed plenty in January.
question: What is the writer's main point?
correct: The app learned from what the writer watched when tired, and now shows that all day.
wrong1: The app knows the writer better than the writer does, because it sees what gets watched.
wrong2: The app would suit the writer better if the writer stopped using it late at night.
wrong3: The app is to blame, because it pushed strange videos that the writer never asked for.
explanation: In paragraph 2, the writer watches driveway videos "At one in the morning". In paragraph 3 they appear "even at lunchtime", when the daytime self is "hoping for Spanish".
source: Original. Imagined student and unnamed app; no claims about any real company.
question2: Why did the writer write this text?
correct2: To explain how a video feed ended up so different from what the writer chose.
wrong1_2: To explain how a stressful exam period changed the kind of videos the writer enjoys.
wrong2_2: To criticise a video app for showing the writer videos the writer never searched for.
wrong3_2: To share a funny story about a strange habit the writer picked up late at night.
explanation2: The writer follows the feed from January, through the exam nights, to "mostly driveways" now, and shows what caused the change.

title: Six Minutes on Platform 2
passage:
On Monday the screen on Platform 2 was broken. Passengers walked to the edge, stared down the dark tunnel, walked back and checked their phones for news. One man asked a stranger if she knew anything. She didn't. The train came after four minutes, and everyone got on looking tired and annoyed.

On Tuesday the screen worked. It said "Next train: 6 min", which was worse news than Monday's wait. Yet the people under it opened books, finished their coffee and talked to each other. Nobody looked down the tunnel, because nobody needed to. Six minutes had become a small piece of free time.

By Friday the screen had a new fault. It said "2 min" for nine minutes. Passengers looked at it, then at the tunnel, then back at it, and soon they were walking to the edge again. This time they were even angrier than on Monday, and two of them complained to the staff about the screen, not the train.
question: What is the writer's main point?
correct: Waiting is easier when people believe the time they are told, even a longer one.
wrong1: Waiting is easier when people find something to do, even if the wait is longer.
wrong2: Waiting feels worst when the train comes much later than the screen said it would.
wrong3: Waiting is easier when the screen shows a short and exact time for the train.
explanation: On Monday, with no news, people looked "tired and annoyed"; on Tuesday a longer wait became "a small piece of free time"; on Friday a number nobody could trust made them "even angrier than on Monday".
source: Original. Imagined station platform and passengers.
question2: How is the passage organised?
correct2: The same platform on three days, with the screen behaving differently each time.
wrong1_2: A problem on a platform, a screen that solves it, then proof that it works.
wrong2_2: The case for station screens, the case against them, then a verdict.
wrong3_2: Two groups of passengers compared, then advice on how to wait calmly.
explanation2: The passage moves from Monday's broken screen to Tuesday's working one, and then to Friday's screen that showed the wrong time.

title: Five Days, No Photos
passage:
Last spring I spent five days in Lisbon without taking a single photo. I had read many times that cameras stop us from really seeing things, and that we remember more when we just look. So my phone stayed in my bag.

It was a lovely trip. I sat in squares for an hour at a time, watched old men play cards and noticed the painted tiles on the walls, which I would have walked straight past while looking for a good picture. I had never enjoyed a holiday so much.

The problem came a year later, when a friend asked about it. I could remember very little: a yellow tram, a café, rain one evening. My trip to Rome two years earlier, with three hundred photos, is still full of names and faces, because I look through the pictures every few months. I still have the tiles, in a way. I can tell you they were blue. I just can't tell you where.
question: Which sentence best sums up what the writer is saying?
correct: Going without photos made the trip better to live through but harder to remember.
wrong1: Going without photos helped the writer notice more but left nothing to show friends.
wrong2: Going without photos made the trip both more enjoyable and easier to remember.
wrong3: Going without photos was a mistake, because a trip without pictures is soon forgotten.
explanation: Without photos the writer "had never enjoyed a holiday so much", but a year later "could remember very little", unlike the Rome trip, which the pictures keep alive.
source: Original. Imagined blog writer and trips. Lisbon's yellow trams and painted wall tiles (azulejos, often blue and white) are real and well known.
question2: Why did the writer write this text?
correct2: To test the advice to stop taking photos on holiday.
wrong1_2: To describe the sights of a holiday in Lisbon in detail.
wrong2_2: To persuade readers to leave their phones in their bags.
wrong3_2: To explain why people take so many photos on holiday.
explanation2: The writer follows advice they "had read many times" and reports what happened, both on the trip and a year later.

title: The Grey Socks
passage:
Before every match, our goalkeeper puts on his left boot first, touches the crossbar three times and wears the same grey socks he wore when we won the cup two years ago. The rest of the team laughs at him. I used to laugh too.

Now I think he is doing something clever. In the minutes before a game, a nervous mind goes looking for things to worry about. Give it a list of small, familiar jobs, such as boot, crossbar, socks, and there is less room for fear. Players in many sports have routines like this, and they often say the same thing: it helps them feel calm and ready.

Last month the socks went missing in the wash. Sure that he could not play well without them, he spent the whole warm-up searching the changing room, then played badly and said it was because of the socks. I think it was because of the warm-up.
question: Which sentence best sums up what the writer is saying?
correct: Pre-match routines calm players, but believing they bring luck makes them risky.
wrong1: Pre-match routines calm players because believing in luck makes them feel safe.
wrong2: Pre-match routines are harmless habits that make no real difference to a game.
wrong3: Pre-match routines calm players, but only as long as nothing in them goes missing.
explanation: In paragraph 2 the routine leaves "less room for fear", but in paragraph 3 the goalkeeper believes he "could not play well without" his socks and misses his warm-up looking for them.
source: Original. Imagined team and goalkeeper. Athletes in many sports describe pre-match routines as helping them feel calm; no study is cited.
question2: What is the writer mainly trying to do?
correct2: To defend a habit that other people often laugh at.
wrong1_2: To make fun of a teammate's strange habits before matches.
wrong2_2: To give advice on choosing a good routine before a match.
wrong3_2: To explain why the goalkeeper played badly in one game.
explanation2: The writer says the goalkeeper "is doing something clever" while the rest of the team laughs at him.

title: Number 47
passage:
The fish counter at our town market used to be famous for arguments. There was no line, just a crowd. Customers pushed forward, called out over each other's heads and accused strangers of jumping ahead. Visitors said the people of the town were simply rude.

Then the market bought a machine that gives out paper tickets with numbers, and a screen above the counter now shows which number is being served. Nobody can jump ahead any more, and nobody needs to watch the crowd to defend their place. Within a month the arguments had almost stopped. People take a ticket, stand back and wait. Some even chat with the person one number behind them.

It would be nice to say that the town learned good manners. But on Saturday morning, walk across the road to the bread stall, which has no machine. The same customers are there, pushing forward and calling out over each other's heads, with their fish tickets still in their pockets.
question: What is the writer's main point?
correct: The tickets ended the arguments by protecting everyone's place, not by changing people.
wrong1: The tickets ended the arguments by slowly teaching the town's customers better manners.
wrong2: The tickets ended the arguments by giving waiting customers a reason to chat.
wrong3: The tickets ended the arguments by making the wait shorter, not by changing people.
explanation: With tickets, "nobody can jump ahead any more" and the arguments stopped, but at the bread stall "the same customers are there", still pushing.
source: Original. Imagined market, fish counter and bread stall.
question2: How is the passage organised?
correct2: A problem, the change that ended it, then a look at a stall nearby.
wrong1_2: A problem, several attempts that failed, then the idea that finally worked.
wrong2_2: Two market stalls compared, then a judgement on which is better.
wrong3_2: One customer's visit to the market, from the fish counter to the bread stall.
explanation2: Paragraph 1 describes the arguments, paragraph 2 the ticket machine that ended them, and paragraph 3 the bread stall across the road.

title: The Bread Machine
passage:
In my kitchen cupboard there is a bread machine. I bought it six years ago, picturing slow Sunday mornings and the smell of warm bread, and I have used it twice. Every time I clear out the cupboards, I take it out, look at it and put it back. I might need it one day, I tell myself.

My friends have their own versions. Lena keeps a guitar she has not touched since university. Tomas has a pair of running shoes, still in the box. Ask them why, and they give my answer: they might need them. Yet all three of us throw away old cables and chargers without a second thought, and those are things we really might need.

Last month I finally gave the machine to a neighbour. It was harder than it should have been for something I had used twice. When I closed the cupboard door on the empty space, it felt less like tidying and more like saying goodbye to Sunday mornings that never happened.
question: What does the writer want readers to understand?
correct: People keep unused things because letting them go means giving up on a plan.
wrong1: People keep unused things because they believe they may need them one day.
wrong2: People keep unused things because they remind them of happy times in the past.
wrong3: People keep unused things because giving them away feels like wasting the money they cost.
explanation: The writer bought the machine "picturing slow Sunday mornings", throws away things "we really might need", and giving it away felt like "saying goodbye to Sunday mornings that never happened".
source: Original. Imagined columnist and friends.
question2: How does the writer build the passage?
correct2: The writer's own habit, others like it, then what happened when it changed.
wrong1_2: A problem in the home, three ways to solve it, then the best one.
wrong2_2: A common belief about tidying, evidence against it, then advice for readers.
wrong3_2: The story of one machine, from the day it was bought until today.
explanation2: It starts with the writer's bread machine, adds the friends' guitar and running shoes, and ends with the writer finally giving the machine away.

title: Knitting the News
passage:
My grandmother can knit a scarf while following the evening news, and she never drops a stitch or misses a story. So I have never quite believed people who say the human brain cannot do two things at once. Most of us walk and talk, or cook and listen to the radio, every day.

Look at how she does it. She has been knitting for sixty years, and her hands know the pattern without her. Walking is the same for nearly everyone. The brain is really doing one thing, and the body is quietly doing the other.

Watch what happens at a busy crossing, though. Your friend stops talking in the middle of a sentence, looks left and right, crosses, and only then goes on. Give my grandmother a new pattern with difficult instructions and the television goes off at once. She says it is too noisy.
question: What is the writer's main point?
correct: Doing two things at once works until both of them need real attention.
wrong1: Doing two things at once is possible only for people with years of practice.
wrong2: Doing two things at once is impossible, however simple the two jobs are.
wrong3: Doing two things at once is fine at home but dangerous on busy streets.
explanation: Two jobs work together when the body does one alone, like hands that "know the pattern without her", but at "a busy crossing" or with "a new pattern with difficult instructions", one job has to stop.
source: Original. Imagined grandmother. That a well-practised, automatic task can be combined with another task, while two demanding tasks get in each other's way, is widely accepted; no study is cited.
question2: Why did the writer write this text?
correct2: To correct a popular claim about the brain using everyday examples.
wrong1_2: To describe how the writer's grandmother learned to knit so well.
wrong2_2: To warn readers about the danger of talking while crossing roads.
wrong3_2: To argue that practice lets people do any two things at once.
explanation2: The writer has "never quite believed" that the brain cannot do two things at once, and uses knitting and walking to show when it can and when it cannot.

title: Guessing the Ox
passage:
Your article on Saturday told the famous story of a farm show in Plymouth, England, in 1906, where about 800 people paid to guess the weight of an ox. Many guesses were far off, but the middle guess of all of them was almost exactly right. Your writer took this to mean that groups are wiser than individuals.

I run a small building company, and our meetings suggest the opposite. When we estimate how long a job will take, our most experienced manager usually speaks first. Then everyone else moves their number towards hers. For years, almost every job finished weeks late.

But the people at the show did not discuss the ox. Each of them wrote a guess on a ticket alone. So last month we tried the same: everyone writes down a number before anyone speaks, and only then do we talk. Our last job finished two days early. Nobody in the office can remember that happening before.
question: What does the writer want readers to understand?
correct: A group guesses well only if each member decides alone before anyone talks.
wrong1: A group guesses better than any one person, as the show in 1906 showed.
wrong2: A group guesses worse than one experienced person who knows the work.
wrong3: A group guesses badly because its senior members know less than they think.
explanation: At the office everyone "moves their number towards hers" and jobs run late, but at the show each person guessed "on a ticket alone", and when the office copied this, a job "finished two days early".
source: The ox-weighing competition is real: Francis Galton described it in Nature (1907), from a fair in Plymouth, England, in 1906, with about 800 tickets; the middle (median) guess was within about 1% of the true weight. The letter writer, company and newspaper article are imagined.
question2: How is the passage organised?
correct2: An article's claim, the writer's own experience, then a change that worked.
wrong1_2: A problem at work, several failed attempts to fix it, then a solution.
wrong2_2: The case for group decisions, the case against, then the writer's verdict.
wrong3_2: A problem at work, then a famous story from history that explains it.
explanation2: The letter starts with the article's story of the show, moves to meetings that "suggest the opposite", and ends with a new way of guessing.

title: My Cousin's Secret
passage:
My cousin Mira studied for six hours a day before her final exams last year and got the best marks in her school. My aunt says Mira was born with a strong mind. The rest of the family agrees, and so, until this summer, did I.

Then I spent a week at her flat. Her phone lives in a kitchen drawer, switched off, until eight in the evening. There is no television. Her desk faces a bare wall, and on it there is nothing but the book she is reading. All day long, nothing in the flat asks for her attention.

On the last weekend we went to a holiday house with fast internet and a huge screen, and Mira watched a whole series in two days. When I told my aunt, she said that putting a phone in a drawer every morning takes a strong mind too. Mira just laughed. She does it half asleep, she says, before she has time to argue with herself.
question: Which sentence best sums up what the writer is saying?
correct: Mira's hard work comes from arranging her home so that nothing distracts her.
wrong1: Mira's hard work comes from strict rules that she forces herself to follow every day.
wrong2: Mira's hard work comes from a strong mind that she was born with.
wrong3: Mira's hard work at home is spoiled whenever she goes away on holiday.
explanation: At home "nothing in the flat asks for her attention"; on holiday, with a huge screen, she "watched a whole series in two days"; and she puts her phone away "half asleep", without a fight.
source: Original. Imagined cousin, aunt and family.
question2: What is the writer mainly trying to do?
correct2: To question the explanation the family gives for a cousin's exam success.
wrong1_2: To praise a cousin for working harder than anyone else in the family.
wrong2_2: To give students advice on how to prepare for their exams.
wrong3_2: To describe a holiday that the writer spent with a cousin.
explanation2: The family says Mira "was born with a strong mind", and the writer's week with her points to a different reason.

title: The Song in the Taxi
passage:
The first time I heard the song, in a taxi in June, I thought it was the worst thing on the radio. The singer sounded bored, and the chorus was one word, repeated eleven times. I asked the driver to change the station.

But it was everywhere that summer: in shops, at the gym, in my sister's car. By July I was humming it. By August I had added it to my favourites and was telling friends it was secretly clever, though I couldn't say exactly how.

In September a café near my office started playing it every hour. Now I leave the room when it comes on. And when I look through the rest of my favourites, I notice how many of them I first heard in a shop, or in somebody else's car.
question: Which sentence best sums up what the writer is saying?
correct: The writer's liking for songs grows the more they are heard, up to a point.
wrong1: The writer's liking for songs grows as their hidden cleverness slowly becomes clear.
wrong2: The writer's liking for songs turns into dislike once they are played too often.
wrong3: The writer's first opinion of a new song is usually wrong and changes with time.
explanation: The song went from "the worst thing on the radio" to a favourite as it played "everywhere", then became too much when a café played it "every hour".
source: Original. Imagined song and writer. That people tend to like things more as they become familiar, up to a point, is well established; no study is named.
question2: Why did the writer write this text?
correct2: To use one song to suggest where the writer's own taste comes from.
wrong1_2: To review a popular song and explain why it is cleverer than it seems.
wrong2_2: To complain that cafés and shops play the same music all day.
wrong3_2: To recommend a song that most listeners dislike the first time.
explanation2: The story of one song leads the writer to notice how many favourites were first heard "in a shop, or in somebody else's car".

title: Three Alarms
passage:
Three alarms and a parent: that was what it took to get our fifteen-year-old son out of bed every school morning last year. We did what the school's leaflet told us to do. His phone stayed in the kitchen after nine, and his light went off at ten. He lay awake until midnight anyway, staring at the ceiling.

At first we blamed him. Then we learned that this is normal. In the teenage years the body's clock moves later, so many teenagers are not sleepy until around eleven or even later. Sending him to bed at ten was like asking an adult to fall asleep at eight in the evening.

This term the school is trying a later start, at half past nine. Some nights he still falls asleep at midnight. But he gets up with one alarm, eats breakfast, and his teachers say he even talks in morning lessons, which is more than he does at home.
question: What is the writer's main point?
correct: A later start helped where early bedtimes failed, because teenage body clocks run late.
wrong1: Early bedtimes cannot help teenagers, because their body clocks make them sleepy too late.
wrong2: A later start helped because teenagers need much more sleep than adults do.
wrong3: A later start helped because it let teenagers fall asleep earlier in the evening.
explanation: The early bedtime failed because a teenager's clock "moves later", and the later start helped even though "some nights he still falls asleep at midnight".
source: Original letter; family and school imagined. That the body clock shifts later during the teenage years is well established in sleep research.
question2: How is the passage organised?
correct2: A family's problem, what they tried, what they learned, then what changed.
wrong1_2: A problem at home, the reason for it, then advice for other parents.
wrong2_2: The school's rules for sleep, the case against them, then a verdict.
wrong3_2: A common belief about lazy teenagers, evidence for it, then a warning.
explanation2: The parents try the school's bedtime rules, learn about the teenage body clock, and then describe the school's later start.

title: The Box by the Door
passage:
At Tallow, a small restaurant near the river, a waiter takes your phone at the door and locks it in a wooden box. The owners say they want people to talk to each other again, and for the first ten minutes of my visit it worked beautifully. Couples leaned in. A family by the window laughed at something that wasn't on a screen.

Then the food arrived, and something odd happened. With nothing else to look at, people looked at their plates for a long time. They chewed slowly. I noticed that the fish was a little dry and the sauce was mostly butter. At the next table, a man pushed his potatoes around and said quietly, "Is that it?"

On a normal evening, half the room would be answering messages, and a dry piece of fish would pass without comment. At Tallow there was nothing to do but eat it. I admire the rule. I'm less sure the kitchen thought it through.
question: What is the writer's main point?
correct: Without phones, diners looked closely at the food, and it was not good enough for that.
wrong1: Without phones, diners grew bored, so they found fault with food that was really fine.
wrong2: Without phones, diners talked to each other more, so the rule did what it promised.
wrong3: Without phones, diners ate more slowly, so they enjoyed their food more than usual.
explanation: The box is meant to get people to "talk to each other again", but in paragraph 2 they "looked at their plates" and found the fish "a little dry". Paragraph 3 shows that phones usually let food like this "pass without comment".
source: Original. Imagined restaurant (Tallow) and visit.
question2: How is the passage organised?
correct2: A rule and its aim, a scene at the tables, then a comparison with normal evenings.
wrong1_2: A problem with phones, a rule to solve it, then proof that the rule works.
wrong2_2: A rule working at first, then failing, then a call to get rid of it.
wrong3_2: Each course of the meal described in turn, from the first dish to the last one.
explanation2: Paragraph 1 gives the rule and its aim, paragraph 2 shows the tables, and paragraph 3 compares this with "a normal evening".

title: One Tea, Four Hours
passage:
The owner of Pip's, the little café on my street, knew my name by my second visit. She remembers that I take oat milk and asks how my exams are going. The coffee is excellent, and the lemon cake is the best in town.

That is exactly why I can't study there. After an hour with one cup, I can feel her noticing. Nobody says anything, but my table could seat two paying customers, so I order a second coffee I don't want, then a slice of cake, and leave after ninety minutes feeling guilty.

At Beanline, the chain café by the station, the coffee is fine and the music is too loud. No one there knows my name, and no one ever will. Last week I sat there for four hours with one tea, and nobody looked up. I know Pip's needs my money more than Beanline does. I still take my laptop to the station.
question: Which sentence best sums up what the writer is saying?
correct: The writer studies at the chain because at the local café, friendliness feels like being watched.
wrong1: The writer studies at the chain because the drinks and cakes at the local café cost too much.
wrong2: The writer studies at the chain because the local café is too small and too busy.
wrong3: The writer studies at the chain because chain cafés treat their customers better than local ones.
explanation: At Pip's the owner "knew my name", and in paragraph 2 the writer can "feel her noticing" and orders "a second coffee I don't want". At Beanline "nobody looked up".
source: Original. Imagined cafés (Pip's and the chain Beanline); not based on any real chain.
question2: Why did the writer write this text?
correct2: To compare two cafés and explain why the writer studies at one.
wrong1_2: To recommend a small local café for its coffee and lemon cake.
wrong2_2: To criticise a chain café for its loud music and ordinary coffee.
wrong3_2: To persuade students to study at chain cafés rather than local ones.
explanation2: The writer describes Pip's and Beanline in turn and ends by saying where the writer takes a laptop to study.

title: Goodbye, Thursday Stew
passage:
The grey stew came every Thursday for six years. At Hillcrest School it was famous. Students drew it in the backs of their exercise books, and older students warned new ones about it on their first day. When the canteen announced a new menu this term, people actually cheered.

I have to be fair: the new food is much better. There's a noodle bowl that's properly spicy, the bread is fresh every morning, and the queue moves twice as fast. I've eaten everything on the menu and liked most of it.

But lunch is quieter now. Nobody groans when they reach the counter, and when I ask my friends about the food, they say "fine" and change the subject. Last week some students in their final year asked the cook, half joking, if the stew could come back for one day before they leave. She thought they were being rude. They weren't.
question: What does the writer want readers to understand?
correct: The bad stew gave students a shared joke, and the better new menu has lost that.
wrong1: Students miss the stew because, despite all the jokes, they really liked its taste.
wrong2: The new menu is a success, because the food is better and the queue moves faster.
wrong3: Students complain about the new menu because they find it hard to accept change.
explanation: In paragraph 1 students "drew it" and "warned new ones about it", so the stew was something they shared. In paragraph 3, now the food is better, "lunch is quieter now".
source: Original. Imagined school canteen and student blog.
question2: How does the writer build the passage?
correct2: A famous dish, an honest view of what replaced it, then how lunch feels now.
wrong1_2: A problem in the canteen, the students' complaints, then the cook's solution.
wrong2_2: The old menu and the new one compared dish by dish, then a final score.
wrong3_2: The story of one school lunch, from the queue to the end of the meal.
explanation2: Paragraph 1 tells the stew's story, paragraph 2 is "fair" about the new food, and paragraph 3 describes lunch "now".

title: Forty Minutes, Not Ten
passage:
The recipes on Ten-Minute Table do not take ten minutes. I tested three of them last week, and the fastest took forty. On screen, the chef, Ines Varga, has every onion already chopped and every pan already hot. Critics have called the show's title a lie, and they have a point.

Then there is my flatmate Joel. For two years he lived on toast and takeaways; in his family, cooking took all evening. One night he watched Ines make a curry in ten minutes and thought, I can do that. He couldn't. Forty minutes later he was still chopping, but by then the onions were in the pan and he wasn't going to stop.

Joel now cooks three nights a week, and every meal takes him about forty minutes. He knows this perfectly well. Last week I asked whether he would ever have started if the show had been called Forty-Minute Table. "Forty minutes?" he said. "Who has forty minutes?" Then he went to put the rice on.
question: What is the writer's main point?
correct: The show's ten-minute promise is false, but it is what persuades viewers to start cooking.
wrong1: The show's ten-minute promise is false, so viewers give up when the meals take longer.
wrong2: The show's ten-minute promise is false, but the recipes are worth the extra time.
wrong3: The show's critics are right that it should be honest about how long recipes take.
explanation: Paragraph 1 admits the title is "a lie", but in paragraph 2 it made Joel think "I can do that". In paragraph 3 he cooks three nights a week, yet still asks "Who has forty minutes?"
source: Original. Imagined TV show (Ten-Minute Table), chef (Ines Varga) and flatmate.
question2: How is the passage organised?
correct2: A fault in the show, one viewer's story, then his reply to a question.
wrong1_2: A problem with the show, the chef's reply, then the writer's final verdict.
wrong2_2: Three recipes from the show tested one by one, then a score for each.
wrong3_2: The case for the show, the case against it, then a balanced conclusion.
explanation2: Paragraph 1 gives the show's fault, paragraph 2 tells Joel's story, and paragraph 3 ends with his answer to the writer's question.

title: Thirty Countries, One Hand
passage:
The poster for the Harbour Food Festival promised "thirty countries, one weekend". I arrived hungry and stayed five hours. I ate a Korean pancake from a paper tray, Brazilian cheese bread from a bag, a Spanish omelette cut into squares and something Greek on a stick.

It was all good. But by the third hour, I noticed that every stall was really selling the same kind of meal. There were almost no tables, so everything had to be eaten standing up, with one hand, on the way to the next queue. Nothing needed a knife, a spoon or more than five minutes.

A cook at the Ethiopian stall told me that at home, her family eats slowly, sharing from one big round plate. Here she was selling the same food rolled up in paper cones. "People can't hold a plate," she said, and shrugged. Three stars for the snacks. I'd still like to know what she cooks at home on a Sunday.
question: Which sentence best sums up what the writer is saying?
correct: Because people ate standing up, the festival showed only the snack side of each country's cooking.
wrong1: Because visitors wanted to try new things, the cooks changed their dishes to suit foreign tastes.
wrong2: Because there were so many stalls, visitors could try food from thirty countries in one day.
wrong3: Because the queues were so long, the cooks served food that was quick but badly made.
explanation: Paragraph 2 says everything was eaten "standing up, with one hand", and in paragraph 3 food shared "from one big round plate" at home is sold in "paper cones".
source: Original. Imagined festival. Real: in Ethiopia, meals are traditionally shared from one large round platter of injera (widely documented).
question2: How is the passage organised?
correct2: A promise and a list of dishes, a pattern behind them, then one cook's example.
wrong1_2: A list of dishes, a ranking of the best, then a score out of five.
wrong2_2: A problem at the festival, what the organisers did, then how well it worked.
wrong3_2: The writer's day at the festival in time order, from arriving to leaving.
explanation2: Paragraph 1 gives the poster's promise and the dishes, paragraph 2 notices "the same kind of meal", and paragraph 3 adds the Ethiopian cook's story.

title: Three Bowls and a Burger
passage:
When Lan's Noodles opened five years ago, the whole menu fitted on one small card: three bowls of noodles, nothing else. I reviewed it then and called the beef broth the best in the city. It was dark and rich, the kind of broth that had clearly been cooking since morning.

Last month I went back. The card has become a twelve-page book with photos: dumplings, fried rice, curries, salads, even a burger. The room is bigger and full every night. I ordered the beef noodles. The broth was thin, the meat was tough, and the noodles had sat too long.

Through the kitchen door I could see the same four cooks I remembered, now working at eight burners instead of two. One was frying rice, one was building a burger, and nobody was watching the big pot of broth in the corner. The burger, I'm told, is very popular.
question: What is the writer's main point?
correct: As the menu grew, the same small team could no longer give the noodles enough care.
wrong1: As the menu grew, the restaurant moved to a bigger room, and the cooking suffered there.
wrong2: As the menu grew, the restaurant became more popular by offering something for everyone.
wrong3: As the menu grew, new cooks arrived who didn't care about the dishes that made it famous.
explanation: Paragraph 1 has "three bowls of noodles"; in paragraph 2 the menu is "a twelve-page book" and the broth is thin. Paragraph 3 shows why: "nobody was watching the big pot".
source: Original. Imagined restaurant (Lan's Noodles) and revisit.
question2: Why did the writer write this text?
correct2: To explain what went wrong at a restaurant the writer once praised.
wrong1_2: To recommend a restaurant's new and much longer menu to readers.
wrong2_2: To describe how a small noodle bar grew into a busy restaurant.
wrong3_2: To compare a restaurant's beef noodles with its popular new burger.
explanation2: The writer goes back to a place once called "the best in the city" and shows what happened in the kitchen.

title: Soufflé, Slightly Late
passage:
Our waiter at Brookfield Kitchen was nineteen and terrified. He poured water onto the tablecloth, forgot our bread and called my friend "sir" four times. Brookfield is the restaurant of a cookery school, and everyone working here, from the waiters to the cooks, is a trainee.

The menu looks like something from my grandmother's photo albums: cheese soufflé, fish in butter sauce, a lemon tart with burnt sugar on top. Food writers have called it dated. The school teaches these classics because every young cook has to learn them first, so the trainees cook them every night.

The fashionable places in town serve small plates and smoke everything. I can't remember the last time I saw a soufflé on a menu. Mine arrived twenty minutes late and leaning slightly to one side, and it was the first I had eaten in ten years. Book a table, bring patience, and order whatever sounds oldest.
question: What does the writer want readers to understand?
correct: Trainees there must cook old classics, so it is a rare chance to eat them.
wrong1: Trainees there are still learning, so diners should be patient with all their mistakes.
wrong2: Trainees there cook well enough to make up for a menu that critics call dated.
wrong3: Trainees there serve fashionable small plates, which makes up for their clumsy service.
explanation: Paragraph 2 says the school teaches "these classics", so trainees "cook them every night". Paragraph 3 says the writer can't remember "the last time I saw a soufflé on a menu".
source: Original. Imagined cookery-school restaurant (Brookfield Kitchen).
question2: Why did the writer write this text?
correct2: To recommend a restaurant even though its service is clumsy.
wrong1_2: To criticise a restaurant for its old-fashioned menu and poor service.
wrong2_2: To explain how a cookery school trains its young waiters and cooks.
wrong3_2: To compare a training restaurant with the fashionable places in town.
explanation2: After the waiter's mistakes, the writer still tells readers to "Book a table".

title: Lasagne, Aisle Seven
passage:
Tonight's restaurant is aisle seven of my local supermarket, and the dish is the Classic Lasagne, £4, served in its own black plastic tray. I removed the film, gave it four minutes in the microwave and sat down at my kitchen table with a notebook, exactly as I would for any review.

As fine dining, it is a disappointment. The pasta is soft, the cheese is shy, and there is no chef waiting to surprise me. Every mouthful tastes like the one before. A great restaurant can change what you think a lasagne is. This one has no such ambition.

And yet I have eaten this lasagne perhaps forty times, and it has never once let me down. It has tasted exactly the same in three different flats, after long shifts, and on the night I moved house with no plates unpacked. No restaurant I have reviewed could promise me that. Four stars, on a Tuesday.
question: What is the writer's main point?
correct: The lasagne never surprises, but its sameness makes it valuable on tired, ordinary evenings.
wrong1: The lasagne may lack ambition, but it tastes as good as most restaurant food.
wrong2: The lasagne shows that restaurant critics care too much about surprise and ambition.
wrong3: The lasagne is worth eating because it is cheaper and quicker than going out.
explanation: Paragraph 2 says "Every mouthful tastes like the one before", which is bad for fine dining. Paragraph 3 turns this round: it "has never once let me down".
source: Original. Imagined supermarket ready meal; no real brand or shop.
question2: Why did the writer write this text?
correct2: To praise a cheap ready meal while admitting it fails as fine dining.
wrong1_2: To make fun of restaurant critics and the serious way they write.
wrong2_2: To criticise a cheap ready meal while admitting it is quick and easy.
wrong3_2: To explain how to cook a supermarket lasagne properly at home.
explanation2: The writer admits it is "a disappointment" as fine dining, but still gives it "Four stars".

title: One Piece of Beetroot
passage:
The first course at Fennel arrived on a white plate as wide as a steering wheel. In the middle sat one small piece of beetroot. My friend Dev took a photo and sent it to his brother with the words "dinner, apparently". Someone at the next table laughed out loud.

The next six courses were the same: huge plates, little food, a lot of white space. Each one looked like a joke. But afterwards I counted: two kinds of fish, a whole duck leg, bread, cheese and a chocolate pudding. Dev, who usually buys chips on the way home from expensive meals, said he couldn't eat another thing.

On a saucer, that beetroot would have looked like a starter. On a plate that size it looked like an apology, and all evening the room was laughing at food that deserved better. Someone at Fennel should go shopping for smaller plates.
question: What is the writer's main point?
correct: Fennel gives diners plenty to eat, but its huge plates make every portion look tiny.
wrong1: Fennel's diners laugh at the food, though it is good enough to deserve their respect.
wrong2: Fennel serves too little food, and its huge plates make that even easier to see.
wrong3: Fennel's huge plates turn each small course into a joke that diners enjoy sharing.
explanation: In paragraph 2 the writer counts "two kinds of fish, a whole duck leg" and more, and Dev "couldn't eat another thing". Paragraph 3 says on a plate that size the food "looked like an apology".
source: Original. Imagined restaurant (Fennel).
question2: How is the passage organised?
correct2: A first reaction, a second look at the meal, then advice to the restaurant.
wrong1_2: A complaint about small portions, the reasons for them, then a solution.
wrong2_2: Each course described in turn, from the beetroot to the chocolate pudding.
wrong3_2: A friend's opinion of the meal, then the writer's own different verdict.
explanation2: Paragraph 1 is the joke about the beetroot, paragraph 2 counts what they really ate, and paragraph 3 suggests "smaller plates".

title: Send Her to Mill Road
passage:
Dear Editor, last Saturday your restaurant critic spent £240 on dinner for two and gave the place two stars. I enjoyed the review very much. Her description of the "sad little foam" on the fish made me laugh out loud on the bus.

But I will never eat there, and neither will most of your readers. When I eat out, it's at the noodle bar by the station or the Turkish grill on Mill Road, once a month, with money I've put aside. If I choose badly, that's my treat gone until next month. Your critic can have a bad dinner on Saturday and a better one on Tuesday, and the newspaper pays for both.

Last night I went through your website: she hasn't reviewed anywhere under £20 a head in two years. Keep the foam, by all means. I'll keep reading. But send her to Mill Road now and then. I'll even tell her which bus to take.
question: What is the writer's main point?
correct: The critic only reviews expensive places, though readers with little to spend need her help more.
wrong1: The critic's reviews are useless to most readers, because they will never eat at those places.
wrong2: The critic writes well, but the newspaper is wasting money on her expensive meals.
wrong3: The critic should review cheap places, because their food is usually better than expensive food.
explanation: Paragraph 2 explains that a bad choice means "my treat gone until next month", while the critic's meals are paid for. Paragraph 3 notes she hasn't reviewed "anywhere under £20 a head".
source: Original. Imagined letter, newspaper critic and restaurants.
question2: Why did the writer write this text?
correct2: To ask an editor to send the critic to cheaper places.
wrong1_2: To complain about a bad dinner at an expensive new restaurant in town.
wrong2_2: To praise a newspaper critic for her funny writing about food.
wrong3_2: To recommend a noodle bar and a grill to other readers.
explanation2: After praising the review, the writer asks the paper to "send her to Mill Road now and then".

title: What the Farmer Found
passage:
Last spring a regional newspaper ran a story under the headline "What one farmer found when he drained his pond". The comments filled up with the usual complaint: clickbait, just tell us. Several people said they refused to click on principle. They missed a car from the 1960s with the keys still in it, and the story of who had driven it into the water and why nobody had reported it missing for fifty years.

An open question is a promise to the reader, as old as storytelling: serialised novels and radio dramas lived on exactly that promise. Had the headline said "Car found in pond", I would have scrolled past, and so, I suspect, would most of the complainers.

The headlines people rightly hate are the ones that break the promise: "You won't believe what happened next", followed by something entirely believable. Each one costs whoever clicks perhaps a minute, and most of us have learned to shrug that off.

What lasts is the lesson, and readers have learned it well. The sites that wrote the empty headlines have moved on to new ones. The reporter who spent three weeks tracing the car's owner got forty comments, nearly all about her headline, from people who had not read past it.
question: Which statement best expresses the writer's argument?
correct: Empty teasing headlines do their real damage to honest stories, which readers no longer trust.
wrong1: Empty teasing headlines do their real damage by wasting readers' time on stories with nothing in them.
wrong2: Teasing headlines do no real damage, since they are a promise as old as storytelling itself.
wrong3: Teasing headlines do so much damage to trust that serious papers should stop using them.
explanation: Paragraph 2 calls an open question "a promise to the reader". Paragraph 3 says readers "shrug that off" when an empty headline wastes a minute, but in paragraph 4 even the honest reporter's readers "had not read past" her headline.
source: Original column. Imagined newspaper, farmer and reporter. General fact: serialised novels and radio dramas commonly ended instalments on unanswered questions.
question2: Why did the writer write this text?
correct2: To defend teasing headlines against the charge that they are just clickbait.
wrong1_2: To explain why newspapers use teasing headlines even though readers dislike them.
wrong2_2: To criticise readers who complain online about the headlines in their local paper.
wrong3_2: To warn newspapers that teasing headlines will make readers stop trusting them.
explanation2: The writer answers "the usual complaint" by calling an open question "a promise to the reader".

title: The Long Wait
passage:
A striker scores, turns away and runs towards the corner flag with his arms spread. Forty thousand people are on their feet. Then, one by one, they turn to the referee, who stands very still with a finger pressed to his ear. For the next two minutes, nobody quite celebrates.

Video review came into top-level football to stop the kind of mistake you could see from the back row: a goal scored with a hand, a foul missed while the referee looked away. On that, it has largely succeeded. Supporters who once raged for a week over one blind decision rarely get the chance now.

The arguments have not ended, though. They have moved. Fans now dispute whether a striker's shoulder was two centimetres beyond a defender's knee, in a still image taken from moving video, judged by officials in a distant room. These are calls no one can make with certainty, which is why they are so easy to argue about.

Something else has moved too: the moment itself. The joy that used to arrive with the ball in the net now waits for permission. Not long ago, that striker would already be buried under his teammates. Now he stands with everyone else, watching a man listen to a voice in his ear.
question: Which conclusion does the passage as a whole support?
correct: Video review removed obvious errors, but moved arguments to tiny margins and delayed the joy.
wrong1: Video review has done more harm than good, since it takes away the joy of a goal.
wrong2: Video review keeps causing arguments because officials in distant rooms often get decisions wrong.
wrong3: Video review was meant to end arguments, but fans argue about decisions as much as ever.
explanation: Paragraph 2 says video review has "largely succeeded" with obvious mistakes, but in paragraph 3 the arguments "have moved", and in paragraph 4 the joy "now waits for permission".
source: Original feature; the match is imagined. Real, widely documented background: video assistant referees were introduced into top-level football in the late 2010s to correct clear errors such as handballs and missed fouls; offside decisions are judged from still frames, checked by video officials who usually work away from the pitch. No specific matches, leagues or people.
question2: What is the writer mainly trying to do?
correct2: To show how video review has changed what happens at a football match.
wrong1_2: To argue that video review has failed to end arguments about referees' decisions.
wrong2_2: To explain how video review works, from the referee's ear to the screen.
wrong3_2: To persuade the people who run football to remove video review from the game.
explanation2: The writer shows what video review has fixed in paragraph 2, then what "has moved" in paragraphs 3 and 4.

title: Sorry, Everyone
passage:
The video always looks the same. A plain wall, very little make-up, a voice a little quieter than usual. "I want to address what happened." Then three minutes in which a famous person apologises to a camera, and in the days that follow, millions of strangers decide whether to accept.

The usual complaint is that these apologies are fake, written by a manager and read off a screen. Some are. But I have watched ones that seemed entirely sincere, a singer's voice breaking, a television cook unable to finish a sentence, and they were received no better. Whatever is wrong with them, it is not mainly the acting.

Consider who is being spoken to. When a television host is cruel to a guest, there is one person, or a handful, who was actually hurt. An ordinary apology goes to them. The video goes to everyone else: fans, critics, advertisers, people who had never heard the host's name until that morning. It asks forgiveness from people with nothing to forgive, and so it turns into a vote, held in comment sections, on whether a career should continue.

The guest, meanwhile, is usually mentioned once, in the second sentence, by first name.
question: What is the writer's main point?
correct: Public apology videos go wrong because they address strangers instead of the person who was hurt.
wrong1: Public apology videos go wrong because they are really about saving a career, not saying sorry.
wrong2: Public apology videos go wrong because fans and critics online judge famous people far too harshly.
wrong3: Public apology videos should be replaced by private apologies to the people who were really hurt.
explanation: Paragraph 2 says the problem is "not mainly the acting". Paragraph 3 says the video goes "to everyone else", and in paragraph 4 the guest is "mentioned once".
source: Original column. No real people; the singer, cook and host are generic, imagined examples.
question2: Why did the writer write this text?
correct2: To explain why the apology videos made by famous people so rarely work.
wrong1_2: To defend famous people who are attacked unfairly online after they apologise.
wrong2_2: To teach readers how to tell a sincere apology from one that is fake.
wrong3_2: To criticise famous people who read their apology videos off a screen.
explanation2: The writer looks at who these videos are really spoken to, and why that makes them fail.

title: The Empty Chair
passage:
Halfway through Market Day, a documentary about the fight to save a hundred-year-old covered market from demolition, the director shows us a chair. It belongs to the city official behind the plan, and it is empty: he declined to be interviewed. We look at it for a long time while a violin plays.

I have no objection to documentaries that take sides. The neutral camera was always a polite fiction: someone decides where to point it, and for how long. Market Day is plainly on the side of the fishmongers and flower sellers, and mostly it earns that position. Its best scene, an old butcher teaching his granddaughter to sharpen knives, makes an argument no speech could.

The trouble starts when the film turns to the other side. The plan has defenders, and the film lets us hear them, briefly: the roof leaks, half the stalls stand empty, and the new building would put homes above the shops. We get these points in a few seconds of a council meeting, cut off mid-sentence, followed by the butcher's tired face.

A film this confident did not need to do that. Five minutes with the plan's most persuasive supporter would have cost it nothing. As it is, I left the cinema on the traders' side, and slightly embarrassed to be there.
question: Which statement best expresses the writer's argument?
correct: The film rightly takes a side, but weakens itself by barely letting the other side speak.
wrong1: The film is one-sided, which is fair, since the official behind the plan refused to take part.
wrong2: The film is one-sided, but its quiet scenes of the traders say more than any speech could.
wrong3: The film weakens itself, because the plan's defenders turn out to have the better argument.
explanation: Paragraph 2 says "I have no objection to documentaries that take sides". Paragraphs 3 and 4 object that the other side is "cut off mid-sentence", leaving the writer "slightly embarrassed".
source: Original review of an imagined documentary, city and market.
question2: What is the writer mainly trying to do?
correct2: To praise a documentary while objecting to one thing it does.
wrong1_2: To criticise a documentary for taking sides, while praising its best scene.
wrong2_2: To support the traders' fight to save their market from being knocked down.
wrong3_2: To explain how documentary makers use music and images to persuade viewers.
explanation2: The writer praises the film's position and its best scene, but objects to how it treats the plan's defenders.

title: Six Downloads
passage:
In 2003, a photographer put thousands of aerial pictures of the California coast online, as a record of how the cliffs were wearing away. One showed the clifftop home of the singer Barbra Streisand, who went to court to have it removed. Before the case, the image had been downloaded six times, two of them by her own lawyers. Once the case reached the news, more than 400,000 people visited the site in a single month.

Two years later a writer named the pattern the "Streisand effect", and the phrase has had a busy life since. A hotel tries to have a bad review taken down and the review spreads; a school bans a student's blog and the blog gains thousands of readers. Each new case is reported with the same knowing pleasure: trying to hide something only makes it famous.

That conclusion is harder to reach than it looks. The cases we hear about are, almost by definition, the ones where hiding failed. When a hotel quietly persuades a website to remove a bad review and nobody notices, there is no story, no catchy name, and no article like this one.

The 2003 numbers are not in doubt. They are simply the kind of numbers that somebody thinks to write down.
question: Which conclusion does the passage as a whole support?
correct: The famous cases can't show how common the effect is, as quiet successes never make news.
wrong1: The famous cases exaggerate the effect, which really happens far less often than people think.
wrong2: The famous cases show that trying to hide something online usually makes it far more widely seen.
wrong3: The famous cases spread so widely because readers enjoy seeing powerful people's plans go wrong.
explanation: Paragraph 3 says the cases we hear about are "the ones where hiding failed". Paragraph 4 accepts the 2003 figures, but calls them the kind of "numbers that somebody thinks to write down".
source: Real, widely documented: in 2003 Barbra Streisand sued photographer Kenneth Adelman and the California Coastal Records Project (aerial photos documenting coastal erosion) to remove a photo of her house; it had been downloaded six times before the suit, twice by her lawyers, and over 420,000 people visited the site in the following month. Mike Masnick of Techdirt coined 'Streisand effect' in 2005. The hotel and school examples are imagined, generic illustrations.
question2: Why did the writer write this text?
correct2: To question how much the famous Streisand-effect stories can tell us.
wrong1_2: To tell how a court case in 2003 gave a popular phrase its name.
wrong2_2: To argue that the Streisand effect happens far less often than the stories suggest.
wrong3_2: To criticise people who try to remove unflattering material from the internet.
explanation2: The writer accepts the 2003 case but asks how much the famous examples can really show.

title: Breaking
passage:
Four winters ago the river came up through my town at night, and I kept the news channel on until dawn. Every hour brought something I could use: which bridges had closed, which streets were being emptied, where the water was expected by morning. At two o'clock I moved my car because a reporter standing in the rain told me to.

Last month a passenger plane disappeared over an ocean on the other side of the world, and the same channel covered it for three days without a break. There was almost nothing to report. The plane was missing and the search had begun. The hours were filled by former pilots and safety experts explaining what might have happened, each theory a little more alarming than the last, beside a map with a red circle that never changed.

In both cases the channel was doing the same thing: staying with a story as it happened. The difference was on my side of the screen. During the search, nothing anyone said could change anything, for me or even for the families waiting at the airport, and the channel kept talking anyway. When the plane was finally found, most of the theories turned out to be wrong. Several I had heard so often that I had started to believe them.
question: What does the writer want readers to understand?
correct: Constant news coverage helps when viewers can act on it, and otherwise fills the wait with guesses.
wrong1: Constant news coverage is useful for local stories but harmful for stories from far away.
wrong2: Constant news coverage harms viewers, because the experts on screen make every story sound more alarming.
wrong3: Constant news coverage is useful in an emergency, but most days viewers are better off without it.
explanation: In paragraph 1, every hour brought "something I could use". In paragraph 3, "nothing anyone said could change anything", and the gap was filled with theories that "turned out to be wrong".
source: Original column. Imagined flood, town and plane; no real event or channel.
question2: What is the writer mainly trying to do?
correct2: To set two stories on the same channel side by side and explain the difference.
wrong1_2: To thank a news channel for the help it gave a town during a flood.
wrong2_2: To criticise experts who guess on television when they have no real facts.
wrong3_2: To explain why rolling news channels keep talking when there is nothing to report.
explanation2: The writer sets the flood beside the plane search and finds the difference "on my side of the screen".

title: Three Stars
passage:
Last year I gave three stars to two films in the same week. The first was a polite costume drama in which nothing went wrong and nothing much happened; I had forgotten most of it by the time I reached the bus stop. The second was a strange science-fiction film with a dreadful first hour and a final twenty minutes that I still think about.

On the review page, they looked identical: three gold stars each, side by side.
