A reader in a hurry, and most readers are, had no way of knowing that one film was safely average and the other was average because it was brilliant and dreadful by turns. Some people would walk out of the second film furious. A few would talk about it for years. Nobody will ever feel strongly about the costume drama.

I am not against stars. For someone choosing a film on a Friday night, a number is quick and honest enough, and I rely on them myself when I choose a restaurant. A five-star film and a one-star film are, roughly, what they promise.

It is the threes that trouble me. Next week I am reviewing a comedy that seems to have been written to offend nobody, and I already have a good idea what it will get.
question: Which sentence best sums up what the writer is saying?
correct: A three-star score can't tell a dull film from an uneven one that some viewers love.
wrong1: A three-star score is unfair to unusual films, which deserve higher scores than safe, forgettable ones.
wrong2: A three-star score shows the problem with giving films star ratings in the first place.
wrong3: A three-star score tells readers little, because critics give it to far too many films.
explanation: Paragraph 2 says the two films "looked identical", though one was "brilliant and dreadful by turns". Paragraph 3 accepts most star ratings, but in paragraph 4 "It is the threes that trouble me."
source: Original column by an imagined film critic; the films are imagined.
question2: Why did the writer write this text?
correct2: To point out a weakness in the star ratings that critics give to films.
wrong1_2: To compare two new films and recommend the better one to readers.
wrong2_2: To defend star ratings, while admitting that they sometimes give the wrong idea.
wrong3_2: To explain how a film critic decides how many stars to give a film.
explanation2: The writer uses two films from one week to show where star ratings stop working.

title: Crying on Cue
passage:
The best scene in Bright Little Thing comes about an hour in. June, a child star of 1950s television, has just been told that her dog has died, so that she will cry properly on camera. The dog is fine. We watch her face while she decides whether to believe it. The shot lasts three minutes, and the eleven-year-old who plays June never seems to be acting.

The film knows what it thinks of the adults around June: the mother counting the cheques, the producer who keeps a list of things that make her cry. It is angry and carefully researched, and when it insists that a child's real pain should never be a product, it is hard to disagree.

Then the poster appeared on the side of my bus. It is that face, from that scene, enormous and wet. The trailer ends on it too, and the director has spoken proudly about how long it took to get. I have no reason to think the young actor was harmed, and her performance is a genuine achievement.

I saw the film again last week. Near the end, the producer pins a photograph of June in tears to his office wall, and I noticed that the cinema had the same image on a cardboard stand by the ticket desk.
question: Which statement best expresses the writer's argument?
correct: The film condemns profiting from a child's sadness, yet sells itself with its young star's tears.
wrong1: The film's makers are as bad as June's mother, because they made a child cry for money.
wrong2: The film is a powerful attack on the adults who used child stars' feelings to make money.
wrong3: The film is powerful, but its advertising gives away the saddest scene before people see it.
explanation: Paragraph 2 says the film insists "a child's real pain should never be a product". Paragraphs 3 and 4 show the young actor's crying face on posters and on "a cardboard stand by the ticket desk".
source: Original review of an imagined film, director and actor.
question2: Why did the writer write this review?
correct2: To review a film warmly, while raising one serious doubt about it.
wrong1_2: To praise a moving film, while complaining that its posters give too much away.
wrong2_2: To argue that child actors need more protection from the adults who film them.
wrong3_2: To criticise the adults who profited from child stars in the 1950s.
explanation2: The writer praises the film's best scene and its anger, then describes something that troubles them about it.

title: Sitcom English
passage:
My Dutch colleague Marieke says she learned her English from American sitcoms. Foreign programmes in the Netherlands, as in Sweden, Denmark and Norway, are mostly shown in their original language with subtitles, so people grow up hearing English on screen every evening. These countries regularly come near the top of international rankings of English skills. Larger European countries that dub foreign shows, such as France, Italy and Spain, score lower. It is a tidy story, and I have heard it told in staffrooms on three continents.

The trouble is that subtitling countries are different in other ways too. They are small, which is largely why they subtitle at all: dubbing a show for a small audience costs more than it earns. Small countries also tend to trade heavily abroad, and need English to do it. And Dutch, Swedish, Danish and Norwegian are among English's closest relatives, sharing much of its grammar and thousands of words. Any one of these could produce the rankings on its own.

None of this means subtitles do nothing. Experiments with individual children have found that they pick up some vocabulary from subtitled programmes, and that seems entirely believable. I recommend the habit to my students. I just don't promise them Marieke's English.
question: Which conclusion does the passage as a whole support?
correct: The rankings prove little about subtitles, since subtitling countries differ in several other ways.
wrong1: The rankings owe more to trade than to subtitles, since small countries need English for business.
wrong2: The rankings are explained by subtitles, since experiments show that children learn words from them.
wrong3: The rankings show that subtitles do nothing, since other differences explain the whole gap.
explanation: Paragraph 1 calls the subtitle explanation "a tidy story". Paragraph 2 lists other differences, any of which "could produce the rankings on its own", and paragraph 3 accepts only a small effect.
source: Real, widely documented: the Netherlands and the Nordic countries mainly subtitle foreign TV, while France, Italy and Spain mainly dub; the Netherlands and Nordic countries rank at or near the top of the EF English Proficiency Index, above France, Italy and Spain. Small audiences make dubbing uneconomic; Dutch and the Scandinavian languages are Germanic relatives of English. Experiments (e.g. Koolstra & Beentjes 1999; d'Ydewalle & Van de Poel 1999) found children pick up some foreign vocabulary from subtitled TV. Marieke is imagined.
question2: What is the writer mainly trying to do?
correct2: To question a popular explanation that language teachers like to repeat.
wrong1_2: To persuade language learners to watch television with subtitles every evening.
wrong2_2: To explain why small countries prefer subtitles to dubbing foreign programmes.
wrong3_2: To support a popular explanation with evidence from experiments on children.
explanation2: The writer takes a story heard "in staffrooms on three continents" and shows what it leaves out.

title: Dear Mr Holmes
passage:
For much of the twentieth century, letters addressed to Sherlock Holmes arrived at 221B Baker Street, asking the detective to help with mysteries of their own. Some of the writers surely knew he had never existed. They wrote anyway.

In 1956, the researchers Donald Horton and Richard Wohl gave this kind of bond a name: "para-social", a relationship in which one side feels it knows the other well and the other has no idea it exists. They were writing about radio and television hosts who spoke to the audience as if to a friend. The feeling was real, but it was also safe. Nobody expected the host to call.

The worry now is that young people's attachment to video makers and streamers is new and unhealthy. Most of it is neither. A teenager who feels she knows the woman who talks about books on camera every evening is doing what her great-grandmother did with a voice on the radio.

What has changed is that the other side now occasionally answers. A streamer reads out a username, replies to one comment in a thousand, says "good to see you again" to a regular. Nobody waited by the door for Sherlock Holmes. Plenty of viewers now refresh a chat window for hours, on the chance that their name comes up again.
question: What is the writer's main point?
correct: One-sided closeness to media figures is old; the rare reply that keeps fans hoping is new.
wrong1: One-sided closeness to media figures is harmless, just as it was in the days of radio.
wrong2: One-sided closeness to media figures is new, and it is especially unhealthy for young people.
wrong3: One-sided closeness to media figures is old, but streamers now trick viewers into caring more.
explanation: Paragraphs 1 to 3 show the feeling is old, and "Most of it is neither" new nor unhealthy. Paragraph 4 says "the other side now occasionally answers", and viewers wait "for hours".
source: Real, widely documented: letters addressed to Sherlock Holmes arrived at 221B Baker Street for decades (the Abbey National building society, whose offices covered the address, employed staff to answer them). Donald Horton and R. Richard Wohl (both at the University of Chicago) introduced 'para-social interaction' in 'Mass Communication and Para-Social Interaction' (Psychiatry, 1956), writing about radio and television personalities. The teenager and streamer are imagined, generic examples.
question2: Why did the writer write this text?
correct2: To use history to test a common worry about young people and the media.
wrong1_2: To use history to show that nothing about online fans is really new.
wrong2_2: To warn parents about the dangers of letting children follow video makers and streamers.
wrong3_2: To explain how two researchers in the 1950s named a kind of relationship.
explanation2: The writer looks at letters to Holmes and 1950s television before saying what is really new about streamers.

title: Brakes. Definitely.
passage:
When my car began making a grinding noise, the first mechanic I tried listened, frowned and said it might be the brakes, or possibly a wheel bearing, or something else entirely; he would know more once he had taken things apart. The second listened for ten seconds and said, "Brakes." I went with the second, and I'd make the same choice tomorrow.

Received wisdom says I was a fool: confidence is cheap, and the loudest voice in the room is merely the loudest. Often that's true. But consider what the second mechanic had staked. Had he been wrong, I would have been back at his counter by Monday, and the story would have reached every neighbour with a car. A garage on a small street lives on its name. His certainty was a bet he could lose.

Compare the commentators who appear on television each January to announce exactly what the economy will do in the coming year. Their tone is identical to my mechanic's. Yet nobody replays the recording in December, and the same faces return the following January, just as sure of themselves. Nobody seems to hold it against them.

It was the brakes, by the way.
question: Which statement best expresses the writer's argument?
correct: Certainty deserves trust when the speaker would pay a real price for being wrong.
wrong1: Certainty deserves more trust from people who fix things than from people on television.
wrong2: Certainty deserves trust when someone gives one clear answer instead of several possible ones.
wrong3: Certainty deserves trust only on small, practical matters, not on big questions like the economy.
explanation: The mechanic's certainty was "a bet he could lose", because a wrong answer would hurt his garage's name, while the forecasters return "just as sure of themselves" and nobody holds their mistakes against them.
source: Original. Imagined columnist, mechanics and television commentators.
question2: What is the writer mainly trying to do?
correct2: To compare two kinds of certainty and judge which deserves trust.
wrong1_2: To reject the common advice not to trust confident speakers.
wrong2_2: To warn readers not to believe forecasts about the economy.
wrong3_2: To explain how to tell a good mechanic from a bad one.
explanation2: The writer sets the second mechanic's one-word answer against the forecasters' equally confident predictions and decides that only one of them is worth believing.

title: Twenty-Four Jams
passage:
In 2000, two psychologists published the results of an experiment at a tasting table in a Californian supermarket. At some times the table offered 24 kinds of jam; at others, six. The large display drew more shoppers, but of those who stopped, only about three in a hundred bought a jar, against roughly thirty in a hundred at the small one.

Few experiments have travelled further. The jam table turned up in bestselling books and business talks, and the lesson attached to it hardened into a rule: offer people fewer options and they will buy more.

Then other researchers tried to repeat the result with many different products. When dozens of these studies were analysed together, the average effect of a larger choice came out close to nothing. Some found that big selections put people off; others, that they left people happier and keener to buy. Choice seemed to overwhelm mainly when the options were hard to compare and shoppers had no clear idea of what they wanted.

None of this makes the original study dishonest. On those days, in that shop, with those jams, something real happened. Somewhere, a manager is still clearing shelves because of it.
question: Which conclusion does the passage as a whole support?
correct: The jam table's real result was wrongly turned into a rule about all choices.
wrong1: The jam table's result was a mistake, since later studies found almost no effect.
wrong2: The jam table's result was real, so shops are right to offer fewer products.
wrong3: The jam table's result holds only when shoppers are offered more than twenty options.
explanation: The lesson "hardened into a rule", but later research put the average effect "close to nothing", even though "something real happened" in that one shop.
source: Real: Iyengar and Lepper (2000), Journal of Personality and Social Psychology: 24 versus 6 jams on a tasting table in a California supermarket; about 3% versus 30% of those who stopped bought jam. Widely retold in popular books and talks. Scheibehenne, Greifeneder and Todd (2010), Journal of Consumer Research, meta-analysis of about 50 experiments: mean choice-overload effect close to zero, with results in both directions. Chernev, Böckenholt and Goodman (2015) found overload more likely with complex options and unclear preferences. The manager in the last sentence is a general image.
question2: Why did the writer write this text?
correct2: To weigh a famous finding against the research that followed it.
wrong1_2: To expose a famous experiment as a mistake that should be forgotten.
wrong2_2: To explain why shoppers struggle when there are too many products.
wrong3_2: To advise shop owners on how many products they should stock.
explanation2: The writer sets the jam table beside the studies that followed, which found an average effect "close to nothing", while saying "something real happened" in that shop.

title: Great Effort
passage:
At the end of each swimming lesson, my nephew's coach walked down the line of children. To those who had swum the whole length, she said, "Brilliant!" To those who had stopped halfway, she said, "Great effort!" By the third week my nephew had cracked the code. "Great effort," he explained in the car, "is what she says when you can't do it."

The thinking behind praising effort is sound enough. Call a child clever and she may start avoiding anything that might prove otherwise; praise the work she puts in and she has something she can control. Many teachers swear by it, even if the research is less tidy than the classroom posters suggest.

But children read praise the way adults read a reference letter: for what it leaves out. Nobody is fooled by a consolation prize for long. The phrase ends up teaching the very lesson it was meant to prevent.

The coach, to her credit, noticed. Now she tells each child what changed: "Kicking from your hips got you two metres further than last week." My nephew still can't swim the length. He has started asking her what to try next.
question: What is the writer's main point?
correct: Effort praise backfires when it only follows failure and names nothing that helped.
wrong1: Effort praise backfires when children can compare it with the praise others get.
wrong2: Effort praise does more harm to children than praise for being clever.
wrong3: Effort praise backfires because the research behind it is less tidy than claimed.
explanation: The idea is "sound enough", but "great effort" became "what she says when you can't do it", and it only starts to help when the coach names "what changed".
source: Original. Imagined swimming coach and nephew. Praising effort rather than ability is widely promoted in schools; the passage notes that the research is mixed and names no study.
question2: What is the writer mainly trying to do?
correct2: To use swimming lessons to criticise how effort praise is often used.
wrong1_2: To explain the thinking behind praising effort rather than talent in schools.
wrong2_2: To describe how one coach became better at teaching young swimmers.
wrong3_2: To argue that children should be praised for results, not effort.
explanation2: The coach's poolside comments lead into a wider point about how adults use praise for effort.

title: Week Nine
passage:
Every autumn, in the ninth week of term, the same student appears at my office door. The essay is due on Friday, it was set in week one, and not a word of it exists. The face changes from year to year. The story hardly ever does.

So I read your report on the homework planner at a local secondary school with mixed feelings. Like many schools, it cuts every long project into weekly pieces, each with its own deadline, and parents receive a message when a piece is late. Late work, the teachers say, has almost disappeared. I believe them, and I don't blame them: a teacher with thirty students cannot wait for each one to discover planning alone.

But the students I see in week nine are not lazy. Most were models of punctuality at school. For years, someone else decided when each piece of work began. Then, at eighteen, they are handed ten empty weeks and a single date, and they discover that the skill they were never asked to use is not there.

My best first-years are rarely the ones who never missed a deadline. More often they are the ones who once missed a big one at sixteen, and had a teacher who asked them what went wrong.
question: Which statement best expresses the writer's argument?
correct: Weekly deadlines stop late work at school but leave students unable to plan alone.
wrong1: Weekly deadlines are the right choice for schools, as they make late work disappear.
wrong2: Weekly deadlines stop late work, but schools should drop them so students learn to plan.
wrong3: Weekly deadlines are not to blame; students struggle later because nobody checks on them.
explanation: With the planner, late work "has almost disappeared", but students who were "models of punctuality at school" later find that the planning skill "is not there".
source: Original letter; university teacher, school and newspaper report imagined.
question2: Why did the writer write this text?
correct2: To warn of a hidden cost in a common school practice.
wrong1_2: To complain that the newspaper's report on a school was unfair.
wrong2_2: To describe how first-year students manage their time at university.
wrong3_2: To defend the teachers who brought in the new homework planner.
explanation2: The writer accepts that the planner works but warns that students later find a skill "is not there".

title: The Leaning Shelf
passage:
The bookshelf in my hallway leans slightly to the left. I built it from a flat box one rainy Sunday, and there is still a screw left over that I have never found a home for. Visitors notice the lean. I notice that I made it, and I would not swap it for a straight one.

Psychologists call this the IKEA effect, after the Swedish furniture company known for flat-pack furniture. In experiments, people who assembled simple storage boxes valued them above identical ready-made ones, and people who folded paper animals rated their clumsy efforts almost as highly as models made by experts.

This is usually filed under bias, and it is one. But it is also why half-built things get finished. Anyone who has spent a winter building a boat or writing a novel needs some unreasonable affection to carry them through the dull middle. A builder who saw the work as coldly as a stranger might never reach the end.

The cost arrives later, when the same affection is asked to act as judge. The team that built its own booking system will still be defending it years after something cheaper and better has appeared. Ask them about it and they will tell you, warmly, about the weekend they finally got it working.
question: What does the writer want readers to understand?
correct: Overvaluing our own work helps us finish it but spoils our judgement of it afterwards.
wrong1: Overvaluing our own work is a common bias that people should learn to correct.
wrong2: Overvaluing our own work is harmless in the home but costly in the workplace.
wrong3: Overvaluing our own work is reasonable, since the effort we put in makes things better.
explanation: Affection carries builders "through the dull middle" of a project, but later, when it is "asked to act as judge", a team defends its system long after better ones appear.
source: Real: the 'IKEA effect' was named by Norton, Mochon and Ariely (2012, Journal of Consumer Psychology); participants valued storage boxes they assembled above ready-made ones, and valued their own amateur origami nearly as highly as experts' origami. IKEA is the Swedish flat-pack furniture company. The bookshelf, team and booking system are imagined.
question2: What is the writer mainly trying to do?
correct2: To argue that the IKEA effect is more than just a weakness.
wrong1_2: To explain why people enjoy building their own furniture at home.
wrong2_2: To warn businesses against building their own systems instead of buying them.
wrong3_2: To describe experiments showing how people judge their own work.
explanation2: The writer admits the effect is a bias but argues it is "why half-built things get finished", before showing its cost when builders must judge.

title: A Swiss Disease
passage:
In 1688 a young Swiss medical student, Johannes Hofer, described an illness he had seen in Swiss people living far from home, among them soldiers serving abroad. They lost their appetite, slept badly and could think of nothing but the valleys they had left. He joined two Greek words, for "homecoming" and "pain", and called the condition nostalgia. For well over a century, doctors treated it as a serious disease.

Today nostalgia is something you can buy. Teenagers queue for vinyl records their parents gave away decades ago; a café chalks "just like your grandmother's" above its cake. The word has lost its pain almost entirely and now means something closer to a warm bath. Most of that change is welcome. Nobody wants a mood treated like a fever.

Hofer's patients suffered, but their suffering had a direction. Nobody writes to an old friend, rings their mother or books the long journey home because remembering feels pleasant. They do it because remembering hurts a little.

A warm bath points nowhere. You get out when the water cools.
question: Which sentence best sums up what the writer is saying?
correct: Today's comfortable nostalgia has lost the ache that makes people act on it.
wrong1: Nostalgia was wrongly treated as a disease and is really a harmless pleasure.
wrong2: Modern nostalgia has lost its value because businesses have turned it into a product.
wrong3: Nostalgia is harmful and should again be taken seriously as an illness.
explanation: Modern nostalgia is "closer to a warm bath", but people contact old friends or go home "because remembering hurts a little", and a warm bath "points nowhere".
source: Real: Johannes Hofer coined 'nostalgia' in his 1688 medical dissertation at Basel, from Greek nostos (homecoming) and algos (pain), describing Swiss people far from home, notably soldiers serving abroad; nostalgia was treated as a medical condition well into the 19th century. The vinyl revival is well documented. The café is imagined.
question2: Why did the writer write this text?
correct2: To use a word's old meaning to question what it has become.
wrong1_2: To explain how an old medical term passed into everyday language.
wrong2_2: To criticise businesses that use the past to sell their products.
wrong3_2: To warn readers that longing for the past can make them ill.
explanation2: The writer uses the painful condition Hofer described to show what today's comfortable version is missing.

title: Popcorn in the Dark
passage:
At the cinema last Friday, the music dropped to nothing, and two hundred people grabbed whoever was next to them. A man in front of me threw popcorn over a stranger. They both laughed, loudly, for much longer than the moment deserved. Afterwards, in the lobby, nobody could stop talking.

The usual explanation for horror's appeal is that we enjoy fear when we know we are safe: the racing heart without the danger. I have never found it convincing. If safe fear were the pleasure, horror would be just as much fun in an empty room as in a packed one, and in my experience it is not. People watch these films in groups, on dates, at sleepovers. A scream is half the fun when someone else hears it.

My sister is the obvious objection. She watches the bleakest horror alone, at two in the morning, with every light off. But by breakfast she has sent me a message describing every scare, and by lunch she has read what several thousand strangers online made of the ending. Then she asks when I am going to watch it, so that we can talk about it properly.
question: Which statement best expresses the writer's argument?
correct: Horror appeals because people enjoy sharing the fear, even when they watch alone.
wrong1: Horror appeals because people enjoy being afraid when they know they are safe.
wrong2: Horror appeals most in a crowded cinema, where strangers can react together.
wrong3: Horror appeals because fans can discuss every scare online, even with strangers.
explanation: A scream is "half the fun when someone else hears it", and even the sister who watches alone shares "every scare" by breakfast and wants to "talk about it properly".
source: Original. Imagined cinema audience and sister. The "safe fear" explanation is a common popular account of why people enjoy horror; no study is cited.
question2: What is the writer mainly trying to do?
correct2: To argue against the usual explanation of why people enjoy horror.
wrong1_2: To describe how a cinema audience reacts to a frightening film.
wrong2_2: To recommend watching horror films with friends rather than alone.
wrong3_2: To explain why some horror fans would rather watch alone.
explanation2: The writer has "never found it convincing" that people enjoy safe fear and argues for another reason instead.

title: Twenty-Two Strangers
passage:
My rule for October was simple: every morning on the train, I would say something to the person beside me. Nothing dramatic, just a remark about the weather or a question about their book. I expected to hate it, and I expected them to hate it more.

Here is the tally. Of twenty-two people, seventeen talked back happily, several for the whole journey. A retired engineer explained bridges to me for forty minutes; a student practised her English. Two answered politely and went back to their phones. Three made it clear that I had made a mistake, one of them by putting on headphones halfway through my sentence.

Those three are the ones I still think about. I can describe the headphones in detail, and I could not tell you the engineer's name. If you had asked me before the month began, I would have guessed the numbers almost exactly the other way round. Every cold stranger I had ever met, it seems, had been filed away just as carefully.

Most mornings my carriage is still silent, everyone in it apparently content to be left alone. I no longer take the silence at its word.
question: Which conclusion does the passage as a whole support?
correct: The silence on trains comes from a fear of rejection that occasional refusals feed.
wrong1: The silence on trains shows that most passengers would honestly rather be left alone.
wrong2: The silence on trains would end if more passengers took the risk of speaking.
wrong3: The silence on trains is a sensible defence against the rudeness of some strangers.
explanation: Most strangers "talked back happily", but the refusals are "the ones I still think about", and the writer had guessed the numbers "the other way round", so the silence cannot be taken "at its word".
source: Original. Imagined blog writer and commuters; the tally is part of the story. No study is named.
question2: Why did the writer write this text?
correct2: To use a personal experiment to explain why commuters stay silent.
wrong1_2: To encourage readers to start conversations with strangers on trains.
wrong2_2: To describe the interesting people the writer met on the train.
wrong3_2: To complain about passengers who are rude to friendly strangers.
explanation2: The writer reports a month of talking to strangers and ends by doubting what the carriage's silence seems to say.

title: Window C
passage:
In the passport office last week, forty of us waited two hours for our numbers to be called. Nearly everyone was looking at a phone. A man near me announced, to nobody in particular, that this was what was wrong with the world: nobody could stand being bored any more.

He had a point, but he chose the wrong room to make it in. Boredom is a message. It tells you that what you are doing is not worth your attention and that something ought to change. In a passport office, nothing can. You cannot leave, you cannot hurry the queue, and staring at the wall will not open Window C any sooner. Silencing a message you have no way of acting on is simply good sense.

The trouble is that a phone cannot tell a passport office from a Tuesday afternoon in a job you outgrew three years ago. That boredom is a message too, and this time there is something to be done about it. Scroll it away every evening and it never grows loud enough to make you move. A friend of mine stayed in such a job for six years. She says she was never bored once.
question: What is the writer's main point?
correct: Numbing boredom with a phone is sensible only when nothing can be changed.
wrong1: Numbing boredom with a phone is harmless, because boredom serves no real purpose.
wrong2: Numbing boredom with a phone is harmful because it keeps people in jobs they dislike.
wrong3: Numbing boredom with a phone is fine in public but harmful when done at home.
explanation: In the passport office "nothing can" change, so silencing boredom is "simply good sense", but in a job you have outgrown "there is something to be done about it".
source: Original. Imagined passport office, man and friend. The idea of boredom as a signal that something should change is common in psychology writing; no study is cited.
question2: Why did the writer write this text?
correct2: To limit a popular complaint about phones to the cases where it applies.
wrong1_2: To defend people who use their phones while waiting in queues.
wrong2_2: To criticise government offices for keeping people waiting so long.
wrong3_2: To argue that time spent being bored helps people become more creative.
explanation2: The writer agrees the man "had a point" but shows it fits a dull job better than a passport office.

title: Dana's First Morning
passage:
On her first morning at the office, Dana hardly smiled. She was nervous, it turned out later, and had barely slept. By lunchtime two of her new colleagues had decided she was unfriendly, and they did not ask her to join them at the café.

So Dana ate alone at her desk. The next day she didn't wait to be asked; why would she? She kept her head down, answered questions briefly and left on time. Each of these was a reasonable response to being left out. Each, to the two colleagues, looked like further proof.

Nobody in this story was being stubborn. The colleagues watched carefully and drew conclusions from what they saw. What they did not notice was how much of it they had produced themselves.

Some first impressions are right, of course. Some people are unfriendly on the first day and every day after it. But the colleagues who misjudged Dana would have felt no different if they had been right. Dana moved to another team after four months. Her new colleagues describe her as the funniest person on the floor.
question: Which conclusion does the passage as a whole support?
correct: First impressions create their own evidence, so wrong ones feel as certain as right ones.
wrong1: First impressions last because people are too proud to admit they were wrong.
wrong2: First impressions are often unfair to people who are nervous on their first day.
wrong3: First impressions are usually correct, because people go on behaving as they did at first.
explanation: Dana's reactions to being left out "looked like further proof" of something the colleagues had "produced themselves", and they "would have felt no different" if they had been right.
source: Original. Imagined office, Dana and colleagues. That expectations can draw out the behaviour that seems to confirm them is well documented in social psychology; no study is named.
question2: What is the writer mainly trying to do?
correct2: To explain, through one office story, why early opinions of people last.
wrong1_2: To warn readers not to judge new colleagues on their first day.
wrong2_2: To describe how one woman found a happier place to work.
wrong3_2: To criticise two office workers for treating a nervous newcomer unkindly.
explanation2: Dana's story shows, step by step, how the colleagues' first opinion kept producing the behaviour that seemed to prove it.

title: Nine Courses, No Questions
passage:
There is no menu at Halde. You sit down, a waiter asks whether there is anything you cannot eat, and nine courses begin to arrive. For the next three hours, every decision is someone else's.

I would not have ordered most of what I ate. I would have walked straight past the bitter chicory with blood orange, and I have spent twenty years avoiding mackerel. Both were extraordinary; the chicory, in particular, did something to the orange that I am still thinking about. Given a list, I would have chosen the lamb, which turned out to be the dullest thing all night.

The same system has a cost. The fourth course, a cold pea soup with far too much mint, was a mistake, and there was nothing to do but eat it. My companion, who cannot eat shellfish, was given plain steamed vegetables in place of two of the best courses, as though the kitchen had run out of ideas the moment its plan was disturbed.

Halde is not for everyone, and certainly not for anyone who needs a kitchen to bend. But last week, in a perfectly good bistro, I opened a menu, read all fourteen dishes and ordered the lamb.
question: Which statement best expresses the writer's argument?
correct: The fixed menu has real costs, but it stops diners ordering only what they already know.
wrong1: The fixed menu works because the chef can make even unpopular ingredients taste wonderful.
wrong2: The fixed menu is worth trying, as long as diners have no foods they cannot eat.
wrong3: The fixed menu suits adventurous diners, but most people would be happier with a normal menu.
explanation: Paragraph 2 says the writer "would not have ordered most of what I ate", and the lamb the writer would have chosen was the dullest. Paragraph 3 admits "The same system has a cost", yet in paragraph 4, given a menu, the writer "ordered the lamb" again.
source: Original. Imagined restaurant (Halde).
question2: What is the writer mainly trying to do?
correct2: To recommend a restaurant while being honest about its flaws.
wrong1_2: To criticise a restaurant's fixed menu while admitting some dishes were excellent.
wrong2_2: To explain how a restaurant without a menu plans its courses.
wrong3_2: To recommend a restaurant to diners who enjoy unusual ingredients.
explanation2: The writer calls two dishes "extraordinary" but also admits that the system "has a cost".

title: The Menu in Four Languages
passage:
In a small town on the Thai coast last spring, I watched a couple from my hotel walk out of a restaurant because its menu was printed in four languages. A menu in English, they explained, meant food for tourists. They wanted somewhere real.

It is an understandable instinct, but it rests on a strange idea of a cuisine as something finished, which outsiders can only spoil. No cuisine has ever worked like that. There were no chillies in Thailand and no tomatoes in Italy until both arrived from the Americas about five hundred years ago. Two of the most "authentic" flavours on earth began as foreign novelties, taken up by cooks who were curious about something new.

The cook in that four-language restaurant, it turned out, made her curry milder for visitors and had started adding a fried egg because so many of them asked for one. Her grandmother, she told me, laughed at the egg for a month and then started ordering it herself.

Some tourist restaurants do deserve their empty tables, serving frozen food to people the owners will never see again. Nobody in those kitchens is changing anything; they have simply stopped caring. The couple found a place with no English menu at all. The noodles, they told me at breakfast, had been cold.
question: Which conclusion does the passage as a whole support?
correct: Adapting dishes for visitors is how cuisines grow, and bad tourist food comes from not caring.
wrong1: Travellers rightly want authentic food, but a menu's languages are a poor guide to it.
wrong2: Tourist restaurants deserve more trust than local ones, since their cooks are more open to change.
wrong3: Tourist restaurants serve poor food because they change their dishes to suit visitors' tastes.
explanation: Paragraph 2 shows "authentic" flavours began as "foreign novelties", and paragraph 3's cook adapts her curry in the same way. Paragraph 4 blames bad tourist food on kitchens that "have simply stopped caring".
source: Real facts: chilli peppers and tomatoes are native to the Americas and reached Asia and Europe after 1492, chillies arriving in Southeast Asia with European traders in the 16th century and tomatoes in Italy by the mid-16th century (widely documented, e.g. encyclopedia entries for 'Chili pepper', 'Tomato' and 'Tomato sauce'). Town, restaurant, cook and couple imagined.
question2: Why did the writer write this text?
correct2: To argue against a common belief about where to eat when travelling.
wrong1_2: To argue that Thai cooking owes its best flavours to the Americas.
wrong2_2: To warn travellers about restaurants that serve frozen food to tourists.
wrong3_2: To describe a meal at a small family restaurant on the Thai coast.
explanation2: The passage starts with a couple who reject a restaurant for its "four languages" and then shows why that test fails.

title: Ninety Minutes on Ferry Street
passage:
At six o'clock on a Thursday, the queue outside Ostra already reached the corner of Ferry Street. Ostra takes no bookings, and critics have called this arrogant: a restaurant making customers stand in the cold to prove its own popularity. I waited ninety minutes, and for most of them I agreed.

Then I started talking to the people around me: a nurse straight from a night shift, two students planning to share one main course, an old man who had spent a year trying to book a table at Ostra's sister restaurant. That one takes bookings online at nine every Monday morning, and is full by five past.

A booking system, in other words, rewards people who plan a month ahead, can sit at a computer at nine on a Monday, or know someone who knows the owner. Ostra's queue asks only whether you are willing to wait. The grilled sardines, when they finally came, were worth it.

The cost is real. Nobody with a sleeping baby or bad knees will stand on Ferry Street for an hour and a half; I watched a man on crutches look at the line and turn away. Every way of sharing out forty tables leaves somebody outside. Ostra just leaves them where you can see them.
question: Which statement best expresses the writer's argument?
correct: The queue shuts some people out, but it is fairer than bookings, which favour planners and insiders.
wrong1: The queue is completely fair, because it gives every diner exactly the same chance of a table.
wrong2: The queue is hard on some, but diners enjoy their meal more after waiting for it.
wrong3: The queue is fairer than bookings because it lets everyone see who is being left outside.
explanation: Paragraph 3 says bookings suit people who "plan a month ahead" or "know someone", while the queue asks only "whether you are willing to wait". Paragraph 4 admits "The cost is real".
source: Original. Imagined restaurants (Ostra and its sister restaurant) and street.
question2: Why did the writer write this text?
correct2: To defend a restaurant policy that many critics have called arrogant.
wrong1_2: To warn readers about the long waits at a popular new restaurant.
wrong2_2: To compare two restaurants run by the same owner and choose between them.
wrong3_2: To criticise a restaurant for making its customers stand in the cold.
explanation2: The writer starts by agreeing with the critics, but after "talking to the people around me" argues for the queue.

title: The Missing Numbers
passage:
The menu at Vell is a single sheet of thick cream paper listing eleven dishes, and not one of them has a price. The owner has explained in several interviews that she wants guests to choose with their appetite rather than their wallet: for one evening, money should simply disappear.

At the next table, a couple spent ten minutes whispering about whether the lobster was "a fifty or a ninety". My friend, who had been looking forward to the duck all week, ordered the soup because it sounded cheaper. Nobody I could see ordered dessert.

You can, of course, ask. The waiter will tell you the price of anything, kindly and without hesitation. But asking means announcing, in front of the person you are trying to impress, that the number matters to you, and almost nobody does it.

It is a shame, because the cooking deserves calmer customers. The duck, which I ordered so that at least one of us would, was the best I have eaten this year. The bill, when it came, was perfectly reasonable. My friend read it twice and then, for the first time all evening, asked me about the duck.
question: What is the writer's main point?
correct: Hiding the prices, meant to make diners forget money, kept them thinking about little else.
wrong1: Hiding the prices troubles only those diners who cannot really afford a restaurant like this.
wrong2: Hiding the prices is a trick to make diners spend more money than they had planned.
wrong3: Hiding the prices makes diners order cheap dishes, so they miss the kitchen's best food.
explanation: In paragraph 1 money should "simply disappear", but in paragraph 2 a couple whisper about "a fifty or a ninety" and the soup is chosen because it "sounded cheaper". Nobody asks, and in paragraph 4 the bill is "perfectly reasonable" after all.
source: Original. Imagined restaurant (Vell) and owner.
question2: What is the writer mainly trying to do?
correct2: To criticise a restaurant's decision to leave prices off its menu.
wrong1_2: To explain why some restaurants choose to leave out their prices.
wrong2_2: To warn readers that a new restaurant is far too expensive.
wrong3_2: To recommend the duck at a restaurant with a short menu.
explanation2: The writer shows the owner's aim of making money "disappear" failing, even though the cooking "deserves calmer customers".

title: Nobody Mentioned the Meat
passage:
Ember does not use the word "vegetarian" anywhere: not on the sign, not on the menu, not on its website. I went with my brother, who believes a meal without meat is a snack, and he did not notice there hadn't been any until the dessert arrived.

It isn't hard to see why. The leeks come blackened from the fire under a crust of salt. The cauliflower is roasted until its edges crackle like pork skin, and the beans arrive in a sauce so rich with butter and smoke that my brother wiped the bowl clean with his bread. Fire, fat and salt: the things he orders a steak for.

The exception is the mushroom "steak", the one dish on the menu that pretends. It is cut thick, seared hard and served with a heavy knife meant for beef. It isn't bad. But for the first time all evening, my brother started comparing, and a mushroom will lose that comparison every time.

He has already booked again. He has also told me, twice, that he will skip the steak.
question: Which statement best expresses the writer's argument?
correct: Ember wins meat-eaters by offering what they love about meat, and falls short only when it copies meat.
wrong1: Ember wins meat-eaters by cooking its vegetables to look and taste as much like meat as possible.
wrong2: Ember wins meat-eaters by never telling them that the food they are eating is vegetarian.
wrong3: Ember wins meat-eaters with most dishes, but should take its weak mushroom steak off the menu.
explanation: Paragraph 2 shows dishes full of "fire, fat and salt", the things he "orders a steak for". In paragraph 3 the one dish that "pretends" is the one that starts him "comparing".
source: Original. Imagined restaurant (Ember).
question2: Why did the writer write this text?
correct2: To explain why a restaurant succeeds with diners who expect to dislike it.
wrong1_2: To criticise a restaurant for hiding the fact that it serves no meat.
wrong2_2: To describe how a brother slowly changed his mind about vegetables.
wrong3_2: To compare a vegetable dish with a meat dish and choose the better one.
explanation2: After the brother's surprise, paragraph 2 explains why the food works for him: "Fire, fat and salt".

title: Three Tacos Before a Shift
passage:
For eleven years, Rosa Medina sold tacos from a cart outside the bus station: three for the price of a coffee, to drivers, cleaners and anyone with ten minutes and cold hands. Last spring she moved into the Hall at Canal Wharf, a former warehouse with a glass roof, long oak tables and a jazz trio on Sundays.

Her tacos are exactly as good as they were. Same recipe, same slow-cooked pork, same green sauce that makes your eyes water. They now cost three times as much, and the people eating them have changed: couples on a night out, groups photographing their plates, nobody in a work uniform. The bus drivers, Rosa says, came twice and stopped.

Critics of places like the Hall usually complain that the food gets worse. Here it hasn't. What has gone is harder to photograph. Outside the bus station, where the cart used to stand, there is now a vending machine selling cold sandwiches.

Rosa, meanwhile, has a roof, a toilet and a fridge that doesn't run off a car battery. She earns more on a Saturday than she used to in a week. When I asked whether she missed the station, she laughed for a long time.
question: Which conclusion does the passage as a whole support?
correct: The move kept the food good and helped the cook, but cost workers their cheap lunch.
wrong1: The move was a success, because the food survived and the cook's life is far better.
wrong2: The move kept the food good, but cost the cook the loyal customers who loved it.
wrong3: The move helped the cook, but her new customers now pay too much for the same food.
explanation: Paragraph 2 says the tacos are "exactly as good", but the bus drivers "came twice and stopped", and in paragraph 3 the cart's old spot has "a vending machine selling cold sandwiches". Paragraph 4 shows Rosa "earns more on a Saturday" than she used to in a week.
source: Original. Imagined cook (Rosa Medina), food hall and city.
question2: What is the writer mainly trying to do?
correct2: To challenge the usual complaint that critics make about food halls.
wrong1_2: To criticise a food hall for charging high prices for street food.
wrong2_2: To recommend a food hall to readers looking for a night out.
wrong3_2: To explain why a street cook decided to leave her old cart.
explanation2: Critics say "the food gets worse", but the writer shows that what has gone is something else.

title: The Chipped Bowl
passage:
In the first series of Home Heat, a retired electrician won with his mother's fish stew, served in the same chipped bowl she had always used. It was brown and enormous, and the judges, who had expected very little, went quiet when they tasted it.

Six series later, nobody brings a chipped bowl. The contestants are still home cooks, as the rules require, but you would never guess it from their plates: dots and smears, a little tower in the middle, a foam on the side. Several mention, proudly, that they have watched every episode since they were children. Each year's winning plates were a little neater than the last, and each new group of contestants arrived knowing exactly what had won before.

In fairness, the cooking is far more skilful than it was. This year's semi-finalists can do things with sugar and butter that would have terrified the electrician, and the judges say so every week. Nobody burns anything any more.

The most interesting moment of the new series came in week three, when a nervous teenager served her grandmother's lentils, unarranged, in a plain white bowl. The judges called it brave. She went home that night.
question: Which conclusion does the passage as a whole support?
correct: Contestants who have studied past winners cook more skilfully, but plain home dishes now lose.
wrong1: The judges now prefer fancy plates because they have grown tired of simple home cooking.
wrong2: The show has lost its charm because the contestants are now professional cooks, not home cooks.
wrong3: The show should return to its first series, when home cooks served their family dishes.
explanation: Paragraph 2 says contestants have "watched every episode" and know "what had won before". Paragraph 3 admits the cooking is "far more skilful", but in paragraph 4 the grandmother's lentils go home.
source: Original. Imagined TV cooking competition (Home Heat) and contestants.
question2: What is the writer mainly trying to do?
correct2: To question whether a cooking show has changed for the better.
wrong1_2: To explain how the contestants on a cooking show are chosen.
wrong2_2: To praise a cooking show for raising the standard of home cooking.
wrong3_2: To tell the story of a retired electrician who won a cooking show.
explanation2: The writer admits the cooking is "far more skilful", then ends with a home cook sent home for a plain dish.

title: Nothing to Hide
passage:
Every seat at Copper faces the kitchen. You eat at a long steel counter with the cooks a metre away, close enough to feel the heat when the grill flares. The restaurant's website calls this "cooking with nothing to hide", and on my first visit I believed it.

On my second, I arrived early and was sent to the toilets along a back corridor. Halfway down, a door stood open onto a second kitchen, twice the size of the first, where six people I had never seen were boning ducks, straining huge pots of stock and peeling what looked like a small mountain of potatoes. None of them wore the neat grey jackets of the cooks out front.

Back at the counter, I realised I had been watching the last two minutes of every dish: the sauce poured, the leaves placed with tweezers, a flame for the sake of a flame. It is skilful, and genuinely fun to watch. I would happily go back for the show alone, and the duck is excellent.

The website still promises nothing to hide, and strictly speaking it is right: the door in the corridor was open. Most diners will simply never walk past it.
question: What does the writer want readers to understand?
correct: The open kitchen shows diners only the finishing touches, so its claim to honesty is misleading.
wrong1: The open kitchen gives a misleading image, because it hides how many people work there.
wrong2: The open kitchen is honest, since anyone walking down the corridor can see the rest.
wrong3: The open kitchen is a good show, but diners should see the back kitchen too.
explanation: Paragraph 1 quotes the promise of "cooking with nothing to hide", but paragraph 2 finds the slow work done in a second kitchen, and paragraph 3 says diners see only "the last two minutes of every dish".
source: Original. Imagined restaurant (Copper).
question2: What is the writer mainly trying to do?
correct2: To test the claim a restaurant makes about its kitchen.
wrong1_2: To criticise a restaurant for the way it treats its kitchen staff.
wrong2_2: To explain how a restaurant prepares its food before the evening begins.
wrong3_2: To recommend a restaurant to diners who enjoy watching cooks at work.
explanation2: The writer tests the website's promise of "nothing to hide" against what a second visit showed.

title: Blackcurrant, Apparently
passage:
The most expensive coffee at Sill costs £9 and arrives on a wooden tray with a small printed card. The card tells you what to expect: blackcurrant, jasmine, brown sugar. I read it, I sipped, and there they were, all three, as clearly as if someone had said them aloud.

My friend Tomasz arrived late and hadn't seen the card, so I passed him the cup and asked what he could taste. He thought for a while. "Coffee," he said. "Quite sour." When I showed him the card, he took another sip and decided that now he could taste the blackcurrant.

This proves less than it seems to. Tomasz usually drinks instant coffee with three sugars, and a more practised drinker might find jasmine where he finds sourness. It is also possible that the flavours were there all along and the card simply gave us the words for them, the way a gallery guide points out a dog in the corner of a painting you would otherwise have missed.

At £9 a cup, I would like to know whether I am paying for the coffee or the card. On my way out, I asked whether I could order the same coffee next time without the card. The barista looked genuinely puzzled. The card, she explained, is part of the coffee.
question: Which conclusion does the passage as a whole support?
correct: One friend's test can't show whether the card creates the flavours, and Sill won't allow a fairer one.
wrong1: The card puts the flavours into drinkers' heads, as Tomasz found when he read it.
wrong2: Nobody can be sure what the coffee tastes of, because every drinker's sense of taste is different.
wrong3: At £9 a cup, Sill is charging for a printed card rather than for its coffee.
explanation: Paragraph 2's test seems to show the card at work, but paragraph 3 says "This proves less than it seems to". In paragraph 4 the barista says the card "is part of the coffee", so the two cannot be tested apart.

title: A Table for One, with Curtains
passage:
The booths at Uno are just wide enough for one person, with a wooden wall on each side and a curtain behind. You order on a slip of paper, a hatch slides open, a bowl of noodles appears, and the hatch slides shut. In ninety minutes I did not see another customer's face.

The noodles are superb: the broth deep and clean, the egg exactly soft enough. And the idea behind the booths is a kind one. The owner built Uno, she says, for people who feel awkward eating alone in public, and there are evenings when I am one of them.

Most of the time, though, I eat alone by choice, and on those nights a curtain is the last thing I want. My favourite solo meals have been at crowded counters: a market stall in Taipei where I watched a cook flip pancakes for an hour, a café in Lisbon where the waiter argued happily with the radio. Alone at a counter, you belong to the room without having to speak to anyone in it.

On the way out, I pulled my curtain back to look at the restaurant. There was no restaurant to look at, just a corridor of curtains.
question: Which statement best expresses the writer's argument?
correct: Uno's well-meant idea hides solo diners away, when eating alone is often best in a crowd.
wrong1: Uno misjudges solo diners, who mostly want to chat with strangers at a counter.
wrong2: Uno is worth a visit for its superb noodles, even if eating in a booth feels lonely.
wrong3: Uno works well for shy diners, but confident ones will prefer a busy counter instead.
explanation: Paragraph 2 calls the booths a kind idea for people who "feel awkward eating alone", but in paragraph 3 "a curtain is the last thing I want": the best solo meals are where you "belong to the room".
source: Original. Imagined restaurant (Uno); market stall and café are unnamed and imagined.
question2: What is the writer mainly trying to do?
correct2: To use one restaurant to make a point about eating alone.
wrong1_2: To explain how a restaurant for people eating alone serves its food.
wrong2_2: To recommend counters in markets and cafés to people travelling alone.
wrong3_2: To criticise a restaurant for making shy diners feel unwelcome.
explanation2: Uno's booths lead the writer to describe the best solo meals, at counters where you "belong to the room".
